Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavirus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisector collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting-specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before harvest periods in endemic agricultural regions.

Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. Keywords Hantavirus, One Health, Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, Rodent reservoir, Ecological surveillance, China, Travel medicine Introduction The epidemiology of hantaviruses is tightly linked to res- ervoir hosts, environmental conditions and human expo- sure, making them a useful model for reviewing zoonotic emergence through a One Health lens. Medically impor- tant hantaviruses are maintained primarily in rodent reservoirs and are associated with two major human disease syndromes: haemorrhagic fever with renal syn- drome (HFRS), reported mainly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also his- torically referred to as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome), reported mainly in the Americas [1–3]. Human infec- tion is usually accidental and occurs when people enter environments contaminated by infectious rodent excreta; however, Andes virus remains the major exception, with documented person-to-person transmission under con- ditions of close or prolonged contact [3, 4]. Rather than cataloguing hantavirus species, this review focuses on synthesising the evidence for how ecological *Correspondence: Xinyu Wang snowmed@gmail.com 1 Department of Infectious Diseases, Huashan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai 200040, China 2 National Medical Center for Infectious Diseases, Shanghai 200040, China Page 2 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 and social processes shape human infection. Key ques- tions are not only which virus is carried by which rodent, but under what environmental and behavioural condi- tions infected reservoirs and susceptible humans are brought into contact. This framing is relevant for the One Health approach, because hantavirus risk can be exam- ined across measurable links including the rodent popu- lation density, reservoir-infection prevalence, climate variability, land use, agricultural or occupational expo- sure, housing conditions, recreational travel and clinical surveillance [1, 5]. China’s long-standing HFRS experi- ence, Europe’s cyclic Puumala virus epidemics and HCPS outbreaks in the Americas collectively provide comple- mentary evidence for understanding hantavirus emer- gence as an integrated human–animal–environment problem. This makes hantavirus disease a useful case for examining how the One Health approach can move from a conceptual framework to measurable surveillance indi- cators and setting-specific prevention. Reservoir ecology and environmental drivers of hantavirus risk The geographic distribution of hantavirus infection is strongly affected by its reservoir-host ecology. Although an increasing variety of hantaviruses have been detected in mammals, medically important hantaviruses are mainly maintained in rodent reservoirs, and many patho- genic viruses show close associations with particular host species or host complexes [1, 2]. This host dependence helps to explain the geographically uneven hantavirus risk, with human disease only occurring where compe- tent reservoirs, suitable habitats and human exposure all overlap. However, reservoir presence alone is insuf- ficient to predict human risk, and the local incidence also depends on rodent abundance, infection prevalence within reservoir populations, seasonal movement, habi- tat disturbance and the frequency with which humans enter contaminated environments [5]. Environmental variability can influence hantavirus transmission by changing the reservoir-host population dynamics and human–rodent contact. Increased rain- fall may enhance vegetation growth and food availabil- ity for rodents, thus supporting their reproduction and survival, while drought, habitat disruption or cold stress may drive rodents into human dwellings, storage areas or workplaces. The Four Corners region of the southwestern United States remains a classic example, where El Niño- associated precipitation led to ecological conditions that favoured increases in deer mouse populations, with a subsequent marked increase in HCPS cases in affected areas [6]. In Europe, Puumala virus epidemics have been linked to bank vole population cycles influenced by for- est ecology, food availability and seasonal conditions [7]. These examples suggest that climate is not a direct cause in isolation, but can influence risk via reservoir ecology and exposure pathways. Because human hantavirus cases often occur after changes in reservoir populations, rodent abundance and infection prevalence can act as early-warning indicators. Long-term ecological studies in Europe and the Americas have shown that rodent population cycles may precede changes in human disease risk [6, 7]. In China, ecologi- cal studies of HFRS have also emphasised the interacting roles of environmental variability, reservoir ecology and human behaviour in shaping disease dynamics [5]. These findings support a practical One Health implication: rodent monitoring should not be treated solely as ecolog- ical research, but as part of an integrated risk-assessment system linking animal, environmental and human health data. Land use, agriculture and human exposure: evidence from China and beyond Land use determines how often reservoir hosts, con- taminated environments and susceptible humans share the same space. Agricultural expansion, crop harvesting, grain storage, peri-domestic farming structures, forest edges and poorly sealed rural housing can increase the opportunities for contact with rodent excreta. A system- atic review of land cover, land use and human hantavi- rus infection risk found that agricultural land use was positively associated with infection risk in several set- tings, particularly in China and Brazil, whereas associa- tions with forest cover, grassland or built-up areas varied by region and virus ecology [8]. This heterogeneity is important, in that land use is not a universal risk factor but rather modifies exposure through local combinations of reservoir species, farming systems, housing conditions and human behaviour. China provides one of the clearest examples of how virus ecology and human activity jointly structure hanta- virus seasonality. In many endemic areas, HFRS shows a bimodal pattern, with a larger autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak. In China, this bimodal pattern has often been interpreted as reflect- ing the coexistence of different virus–host systems and exposure settings. Hantaan virus, mainly associated with Apodemus agrarius, contributes more to field or rural exposure and autumn–winter incidence, whereas Seoul virus, carried by Rattus norvegicus, is more relevant to peri-domestic or urban transmission and spring inci- dence in many settings [9–11]. In Zibo City, HFRS cases peaked during March–May and October–December, illustrating the seasonal human risk pattern [9]. Spatial analyses from the same region further suggested that Page 3 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 spring and autumn risks differed geographically, support- ing targeted seasonal prevention [12]. The link between agricultural activity and HFRS sea- sonality is particularly evident in high-incidence prov- inces such as Shandong. A time-series analysis reported marked seasonality and discussed the temporal cor- respondence between agricultural activity and HFRS incidence: the autumn harvest usually begins in late September, cases then rise rapidly in October, peak in November, and decline in December [13]. The incubation period of hantavirus infection suggests that this pattern is biologically plausible and consistent with exposure dur- ing harvesting, field work, grain handling or temporary accommodation in rodent-infested settings. Together with the smaller spring peak observed in many endemic areas, this pattern suggests that HFRS risk is shaped by seasonally changing combinations of reservoir ecology, agricultural labour and peri-domestic exposure, rather than by a single constant pathway. In addition to agriculture, hantavirus exposure may occur in occupational, domestic, recreational and travel settings. Farmers, forestry workers, construction work- ers, cleaners, military personnel and people entering rodent-infested buildings may experience intense short- term exposure when contaminated dust is disturbed. Recreational exposure can occur when visitors stay in cabins, campsites or enclosed structures with rodent infestation. The 2012 Yosemite National Park outbreak, linked to overnight stays in insulated tent cabins, showed how built environments can convert local rodent ecology into visitor risk [14]. The 2026 cruise-associated Andes virus cluster illustrates a different pathway, with local ecological exposure potentially becoming a multi-coun- try public health problem when combined with delayed recognition, confined travel settings and international movements [15]. Surveillance evidence and gaps across human– animal–environment systems China’s long-term HFRS experience provides an instruc- tive example of surveillance that already contains several One Health elements, even if not always labelled as such. National surveillance has combined human case report- ing with rodent surveillance, laboratory testing and tar- geted prevention in endemic areas. During 2006–2012, 77,558 HFRS cases and 866 deaths were reported in China. Cases were clustered in a small number of prov- inces and occurring mainly in spring and autumn–win- ter seasons, with farmers remaining the largest affected occupational group [10]. More recent national data for 2014–2023 show continuing geographic and virological complexity, with Hantaan virus, Seoul virus and Puu- mala virus among the identified human HFRS-associated hantaviruses in China [11]. These regional contrasts are summarised in Table 1, which compares rodent, envi- ronmental and human surveillance components across China, Europe and the Americas. Despite the value of long-term case reporting, human surveillance alone is inherently too late for hantavirus prevention, and human cases usually only appear after ecological changes, rodent population shifts and expo- sure events have already occurred. Clinical recogni- tion may also be delayed because the early symptoms are non-specific and overlap with leptospirosis, dengue, influenza-like illness, malaria, COVID-19 and other febrile syndromes [3]. This is particularly relevant in rural or travel-related settings, where the exposure event may be remote in time and place from the diagnosis. For surveillance to support prevention rather than only documentation, clinical signals should be connected with rodent, environmental and exposure information. In clinical practice, a compatible syndrome combined with a carefully reconstructed exposure history—such as recent rural residence, crop harvesting, cleaning of rodent-infested spaces, cabin stay or expedition travel— may provide the first actionable signal before laboratory confirmation. The One Health challenge is therefore not simply to collect more data, but to link the appropriate data to timely decisions. Information on rodent density, reser- voir infection prevalence, climate anomalies, agricultural calendars, land-use changes, clinical syndromes and travel or occupational histories is often held by different sectors and interpreted separately. Broader One Health early-warning literature emphasises the importance of bottom-up reporting and grassroots actors for reduc- ing delays between outbreak emergence, notification and response [16]. For hantavirus diseases, integrated early warning should therefore be judged not by the number of assembled datasets, but by whether ecological and clinical signals lead to earlier, setting-specific preven- tion. Future surveillance should therefore be built around predefined risk questions and response thresholds rather than around parallel human, animal and environmental datasets. In resource-limited settings, integrated One Health surveillance should not aim to monitor every possible ecological, animal and human indicator. analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing HFRS in Eurasia and HCPS in the Americas, posing a public‑health threat. Methods: This mini review synthesises evidence on ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges through a One Health lens. analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 是啮齿动物传播的动物源性病毒,可导致欧亚地区的肾综合征出血热,以及美洲的 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,构成显著的公共卫生关注。
analysis_zh.methods: 本小综述通过 One Health 视角综合现有关于 汉坦病毒 疾病生态驱动因素、暴露途径和监测挑战的证据。
analysis_zh.results: 发病率可能受啮齿动物种群动态、气候、土地利用、农业实践、居住环境以及休闲或旅行暴露的影响;中国呈现秋冬季肾综合征出血热高峰和春夏季较小峰值,欧洲的田鼠循环影响 普马拉病毒 疫情,美洲的研究将降雨、啮齿动物丰度与人类暴露关联至病例。
analysis_zh.contribution: 作者建议超越笼统的多部门呼吁,转向基于证据的监测,将啮齿动物、环境和人类数据关联,实现针对特定情境的防控,如季节性风险预警和收获前减低暴露的措施。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未在提供的证据中报告。

papers.title: Human Orthohantavirus infections: From virology and clinical epidemiology to oral biological features and dental practice
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic pathogens responsible for 2 severe clinical syndromes in humans: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), affecting an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 individuals annually worldwide, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), characterized by fulminant pulmonary edema with case fatality rates approaching 40%. Although the systemic manifestations of hantavirus disease are well described, the oral and salivary dimensions of infection have received comparatively little attention in the dental literature. This review synthesizes current evidence on the virology, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, oral complications, diagnostic approaches, treatment options, and dental practice implications of human hantavirus infections. A narrative review with a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar was conducted, supplemented by hand-searching and by consultation of the World Health Organization and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control outbreak reporting. Particular attention was directed toward primary research on salivary immunity, oral fluid diagnostics, and salivary gland tropism. Andes virus (ANDV) antigen has been detected in secretory cells of human salivary glands, and ANDV uniquely resists the antiviral capacity of human saliva, providing a biologically plausible mechanism for its person-to-person transmissibility. Infectious virus has since been recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid during acute infection, although a salivary route of transmission remains an epidemiological association rather than proven. In a cohort of 69 confirmed ANDV-infected cases, salivary secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) was significantly elevated (4.846 vs. 0.333 mg/mL in exposed-uninfected contacts), whereas mucins MUC7 and MUC5B were more frequently detected in exposed-but-not-infected household contacts, a cross-sectional finding whose direction of causation is unresolved. Total salivary sIgA is a non-specific marker of mucosal immune activation and has no pathogen specificity. Oral fluid IgM assays for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity against serum reference, supporting further evaluation of non-invasive salivary surveillance. Clinically, severe sore throat persisting for 2 to 3 weeks and oropharyngeal edema are documented as early features of hantavirus infection. Thrombocytopenia, which may be profound during the oliguric phase of HFRS, confers significant oral hemorrhagic risk. Human hantavirus infection presents with clinically significant oral and salivary manifestations that are directly relevant to dental practitioners. Dental teams should be aware of the hemorrhagic risk in patients with thrombocytopenia, the aerosol risk in patients with HCPS, the theoretical risk of ANDV transmission via oral contact in endemic regions, and the emerging utility of salivary diagnostics. Recommendations for dental practice are extrapolated from medical, virological, and general infection control evidence, rather than from dental clinical research, and are identified as precautionary where that is the case.

papers.title: Vaccines Against Hantavirus Infections: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hantaviruses infections are responsible for a hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome with case-fatality rates up to 50%. While inactivated vaccines are already available in China and South Korea, several additional candidate vaccines are under development. This systematic review summarizes the current clinical evidence on immunogenicity and short-term safety of vaccines targeting different hantavirus strains. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic literature search was carried out to identify randomized and nonrandomized trials of any phase. Data were synthesized narratively within strata defined by vaccine platform, target virus, assay, immunogenicity and safety. Results: Ten trials on 961 adults were included: four single-arm trials on the inactivated vaccine and six early-phase DNA-vaccine trials. One month after last dose, the inactivated vaccine achieved neutralizing seropositivity by PRNT50 in 45.1% of the tested subjects after two priming doses and 55.7% after three, while the corresponding binding-antibody values measured by IFA were 87.3% and 95.7%. Among DNA vaccines, homologous responses reached 100% against HTNV and 83.3% against PUUV with monovalent constructs, whereas dual responses to the bivalent construct were registered in 33.3% and 77.8% of the subjects, when measured through PRNT50 and PsVNA50, respectively. One serious adverse event occurred, most likely unrelated to vaccination. Conclusions: No serious safety signal was identified, although safety remains insufficiently characterized. Measured immunogenicity depends as much on the assay as on the vaccine, and, in the absence of a validated correlate of protection, it cannot be read as a clinical benefit. Future research should prioritize validated correlates of protection and innovative trial designs adapted to low-incidence diseases.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome and can have case‑fatality rates up to 50% (A1).

analysis.future_research: Prioritize establishing validated correlates of protection and designing innovative trial designs suited to the low incidence of hantavirus disease (A12).

Gaps: Assay‑dependent immunogenicity, lack of protective correlates, and limited safety data (A11,A10). Future research: Develop validated correlates of protection and trial designs adapted to low‑incidence hantavirus disease (A12).

papers.title_zh: 针对 汉坦病毒 感染的疫苗:系统文献综述

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 感染导致肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征,死亡率最高可达 50%(A1)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 综述指出,灭活疫苗已在中国和韩国获批上市,而多种基于 DNA 的候选疫苗正在研发中 (A2)。
analysis_zh.current_state: 10 项涉及 961 名成人的试验显示,灭活疫苗产生的中和抗体反应适中,而结合抗体率较高;DNA 疫苗实现了株特异性血清转化;除一次无关的严重不良事件外,未出现明确的安全性问题 (A7,A8,A9)。

analysis_zh.future_research: 应优先建立经验证的保护相关指标,并设计适用于 汉坦病毒 疾病低发病率的创新性临床试验方案 (A12)。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：汉坦病毒 感染导致肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征,死亡率最高可达 50%(A1)。 主要方向：综述指出,灭活疫苗已在中国和韩国获批上市,而多种基于 DNA 的候选疫苗正在研发中 (A2)。 研究现状：10 项涉及 961 名成人的试验显示,灭活疫苗产生的中和抗体反应适中,而结合抗体率较高;DNA 疫苗实现了株特异性血清转化;除一次无关的严重… 不足：免疫原性结果因检测方法而异,尚无经验证的保护相关指标,且安全性数据仍有限,尤其是针对新平台 (A11,A10)。 后续研究：应优先建立经验证的保护相关指标,并设计适用于 汉坦病毒 疾病低发病率的创新性临床试验方案 (A12)。

papers.title: Transmission timing and containment risk in human Andes virus outbreaks
papers.abstract: The 2026 multinational Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina triggered extensive contact tracing and quarantine. Whether intervention on this scale was necessary or sufficient depends on the risk of onward transmission, which can be difficult to estimate early in an outbreak. Using transmission-pair data from the 2018--2019 outbreak in Epuyen, Argentina, and a mechanistic model linking viral growth, symptom onset, and transmission, we estimated that 42.4% (95% CrI: 18.2-69.7\%) of transmission occurs before symptom onset and that the median incubation period is 18.5 days (95% CrI: 16.5-19.5). We simulated outbreaks under an Epuyen-calibrated estimate (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) and a pooled estimate from 15 prior ANDV investigations (R = 0.24, k = 0.39), with intervention beginning after two generations, as in the cruise-associated event. Under the higher-transmission scenario, missing 10% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts resulted in a 29.9% probability of continued spread and a 20.6% probability that at least 5,000 ultimately uninfected people would be quarantined. Under lower transmission, continued spread stayed below 8%. However, the risk of onward transmission could not be estimated precisely from the first several detected cases. These findings therefore support rapid, comprehensive contact tracing and quarantine after large international exposure events despite substantial costs.

Introduction Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus known to be capable of person-to-person transmission, although documented transmission has been confined to a small number of localized outbreaks [1– 3]. ANDV infection is associated with a case-fatality rate of approximately 36% [4], and there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral therapies. Recent increases in ANDV activity in South America have heightened concern about the potential for person-to-person spread [5]. In 2026, a multinational ANDV exposure event linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina led to 13 reported cases and 3 deaths, and prompted extensive international contact tracing and prolonged quarantine of 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries [6, 7]. The severity of ANDV disease and its potential for person-to-person spread may warrant such intensive responses, but evidence on their effectiveness and associated quarantine burden remains limited. Evaluating containment strategies requires a detailed understanding of ANDV transmission dy- namics. Decisions about the scale and duration of contact tracing and quarantine depend on incu- bation periods, the timing of infectiousness relative to symptom onset, and individual-level variation in transmission. Long incubation periods prolong monitoring and quarantine, transmission before symptom onset allows infected individuals to spread infection before they are recognized and iso- lated, and variation in transmission means that a small number of infected individuals may account for a disproportionate share of secondary infections. However, estimating these quantities from outbreak data is complicated by evolving control measures, including case detection, isolation, and quarantine, which alter transmission opportunities over time. The 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak provides the most detailed empirical data on person-to-person ANDV transmission. The original outbreak investigation reconstructed transmission chains, identi- fied superspreading, and estimated that the effective reproduction number (Re) declined from 2.12 before implementation of isolation and quarantine to 0.96 afterward [13]. Most reported ANDV infections, by contrast, arise from zoonotic spillover and are not followed by sustained person-to- person transmission. Transmission in Epuyén concentrated at a birthday party and a wake, in a town of fewer than 2,000 people, suggesting that what distinguishes these outcomes is not where infection is acquired but the number and intensity of close contacts during the brief window around symptom onset, variation in infectiousness across individuals, or both. The relative contributions of contact and infectiousness cannot be resolved from existing investigations, which report secondary cases but not contacts that did not result in transmission. Because incubation can last several weeks, the setting an infected person occupies during the transmission window may differ substan- tially from the setting in which exposure occurred. Transmission potential can therefore vary among cases, locations, and generations of the same outbreak. More recently, a latent-time analysis of the Epuyén transmission-pair data jointly estimated unobserved infection times, generation intervals, transmission timing relative to source symptom onset, time-varying reproduction numbers, and offspring dispersion from interval-censored data [12]. However, it modeled incubation and transmission timing as separate empirical delay distributions rather than as outcomes of a shared within-host process. This limited its ability to represent 2 . Here, we extend the latent-time framework by integrating a mechanistic model that jointly links infection, symptom onset, and transmission [15]. We incorporate the resulting estimates in stochastic branching-process simulations of a multinational exposure event based on the initial timing and magnitude of the 2026 cruise-associated outbreak. Given the variation in transmission observed across past ANDV events, we simulate outbreaks in both high- and low-transmission settings. The high-transmission setting uses parameters estimated from the Epuyén investigation, whereas the low-transmission setting uses pooled estimates from 15 prior ANDV investigations. We estimate the level of contact tracing and quarantine required for containment and quantify the consequences of incomplete or delayed intervention. Results We fitted the within-host-informed latent-time model to 34 cases and 33 reconstructed source- recipient pairs from the 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak in Argentina (Table 1; Figure 1). Transmission was concentrated near source symptom onset, with an estimated 42.4% of transmission events oc- curring before symptoms appeared (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%). The median transmission time was 0.07 days after source symptom onset (95% CrI: (-0.20) to 0.30 days), and the central 95% of transmission events occurred from 0.85 days before to 2.02 days after source symptom onset (Figure 1A). The median incubation period was 18.50 days (95% CrI: 16.50–19.50 days), with a central 95% distributional interval of 7.50–35.50 days (Figure 1C). An estimated 95% of infections developed symptoms by 31.50 days (95% CrI: 29.50–35.50), and 99% by 39.50 days (95% CrI: 35.50–44.50). The median generation interval was 22.50 days (95% CrI: 20.50–23.50 days) (Figure 1B), and the median serial interval was 21.79 days (95% CrI: 21.28–22.18 days) (Figure 1D). Thus, exposed individuals may require several weeks of follow-up even though onward transmission is concentrated within a narrow window around symptom onset. These estimates were broadly consistent with previous analyses of the Epuyén outbreak while providing model-based inference of latent infection times and transmission timing relative to symptom onset (Supplementary Results). The central 95% interval summarizes the expected range across individual infections or transmission events. Transmission timing is reported relative to source symptom onset, with negative values indicating transmission before symptom onset. To characterize the transmission conditions documented across settings, we analyzed 15 pub- lished ANDV investigations. A hierarchical negative-binomial model estimated a pooled reproduc- tion number of 0.24 (95% CrI: 0.12–0.48) and a shared dispersion parameter of 0.39 (95% CrI: 0.19–0.89), reflecting low average but highly variable realized transmission across this broader set of investigations. Together with the Epuyén-calibrated estimates (R=2.12, k=0.316), these results anchored an empirically informed range of ANDV transmission potential. Hereafter, we refer to simulations using the Epuyén and pooled parameterizations as the higher- and lower-transmission scenarios, respectively. The primary analysis reproduced the timing of the 2026 cruise-associated response, with inter- vention beginning on simulation day 35, 26 days after symptom onset in the first detected case. 4 . Tracing failures had substantially greater consequences under higher transmission (Figure 2A). When tracing missed 5%, 10%, 25%, or 50% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts, post-response transmission outside quarantine occurred in 18.9%, 29.9%, 51.1%, and 70.8% of simulations, respectively. Under the lower transmission, this probability ranged from 0.7% with 5% missed to 7.8% with 50% missed. Among simulations with higher transmission and at least one additional post-response infection, missing 10% of contacts resulted in a median of 5 additional infections and a 95th percentile of 49. With 25% or 50% missed, the medians increased to 8 and 27, respectively, and the 95th percentiles to 111 and 351. With lower transmission, the median remained between one and two across tracing levels (Figure 2B). Quarantine burdens were substantially lower under lower transmission (Figure 2C). With 10% of contacts missed, the median number of retrospectively uninfected downstream contacts quaran- tined was 313 (IQR 185–440), compared with 1,821 (IQR 720–4,161) under the higher-transmission scenario. At lower transmission, the median burden fell by 49%, from 329 with complete tracing to 167 with 50% of contacts missed, because outbreaks were small and fewer contacts were traced. At higher transmission, fewer quarantines per case were offset by larger outbreaks and more tracing events, leaving the median comparatively stable but increasing the risk of very large quarantine burdens. Most response activity ended within the initial six-week quarantine period, but breakthrough transmission occasionally prolonged the response under the higher-transmission scenario. full_text_sections.full_text: Transmission timing and containment risk in human Andes virus outbreaks Nyall Jamieson1,*, Rémy Pasco2, Sam Abbott3, Justin Lessler4,5,6, Lauren Ancel Meyers1,7 1Department of Integrative Biology, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, United States of America 2BioFrontiers Institute, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, Colorado, United States of America 3Centre for Mathematical modeling of Infectious Diseases, London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, London, United Kingdom 4Department of Epidemiology, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States of America 5 UNC Carolina Population Center, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States of America 6Department of Epidemiology, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, Baltimore, Maryland, United States of America 7Department of Statistics and Data Sciences, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, United States of America *Corresponding author: Nyall Jamieson. nyall.jamieson@austin.utexas.edu Abstract The 2026 multinational Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina triggered extensive contact tracing and quarantine. Whether intervention on this scale was necessary or sufficient depends on the risk of onward transmission, which can be difficult to estimate early in an outbreak. Using transmission-pair data from the 2018–2019 outbreak in Epuyén, Argentina, and a mechanistic model linking viral growth, symptom onset, and transmission, we estimated that 42.4% (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%) of transmission occurs before symptom onset and that the median incubation period is 18.5 days (95% CrI: 16.5–19.5). We simulated outbreaks under an Epuyén-calibrated estimate (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) and a pooled estimate from 15 prior ANDV investigations (R = 0.24, k = 0.39), with intervention beginning after two generations, as in the cruise-associated event. Under the higher-transmission scenario, missing 10% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts resulted in a 29.9% probability of continued spread and a 20.6% probability that at least 5,000 ultimately uninfected people would be quarantined. Under lower transmission, continued spread stayed below 8%. However, the risk of onward transmission could not be estimated precisely from the first several detected cases. These findings therefore support rapid, comprehensive contact tracing and quarantine after large international exposure events despite substantial costs. 1 . Introduction Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus known to be capable of person-to-person transmission, although documented transmission has been confined to a small number of localized outbreaks [1– 3]. ANDV infection is associated with a case-fatality rate of approximately 36% [4], and there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral therapies. Recent increases in ANDV activity in South America have heightened concern about the potential for person-to-person spread [5]. In 2026, a multinational ANDV exposure event linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina led to 13 reported cases and 3 deaths, and prompted extensive international contact tracing and prolonged quarantine of 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries [6, 7]. The severity of ANDV disease and its potential for person-to-person spread may warrant such intensive responses, but evidence on their effectiveness and associated quarantine burden remains limited. Evaluating containment strategies requires a detailed understanding of ANDV transmission dy- namics. Decisions about the scale and duration of contact tracing and quarantine depend on incu- bation periods, the timing of infectiousness relative to symptom onset, and individual-level variation in transmission. Long incubation periods prolong monitoring and quarantine, transmission before symptom onset allows infected individuals to spread infection before they are recognized and iso- lated, and variation in transmission means that a small number of infected individuals may account for a disproportionate share of secondary infections. However, estimating these quantities from outbreak data is complicated by evolving control measures, including case detection, isolation, and quarantine, which alter transmission opportunities over time. The 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak provides the most detailed empirical data on person-to-person ANDV transmission. The original outbreak investigation reconstructed transmission chains, identi- fied superspreading, and estimated that the effective reproduction number (Re) declined from 2.12 before implementation of isolation and quarantine to 0.96 afterward [13]. Most reported ANDV infections, by contrast, arise from zoonotic spillover and are not followed by sustained person-to- person transmission. Transmission in Epuyén concentrated at a birthday party and a wake, in a town of fewer than 2,000 people, suggesting that what distinguishes these outcomes is not where infection is acquired but the number and intensity of close contacts during the brief window around symptom onset, variation in infectiousness across individuals, or both. The relative contributions of contact and infectiousness cannot be resolved from existing investigations, which report secondary cases but not contacts that did not result in transmission. Because incubation can last several weeks, the setting an infected person occupies during the transmission window may differ substan- tially from the setting in which exposure occurred. Transmission potential can therefore vary among cases, locations, and generations of the same outbreak. More recently, a latent-time analysis of the Epuyén transmission-pair data jointly estimated unobserved infection times, generation intervals, transmission timing relative to source symptom onset, time-varying reproduction numbers, and offspring dispersion from interval-censored data [12]. However, it modeled incubation and transmission timing as separate empirical delay distributions rather than as outcomes of a shared within-host process. This limited its ability to represent 2 . papers.title: Hantavirus species detection from viral genome sequences using explainable artificial intelligence techniques
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are important zoonotic pathogens associated with severe human diseases, including hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recognized the importance of strengthening hantavirus surveillance and early detection because of their public health impact. Nevertheless, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based approaches for hantavirus species identification from viral genome sequences remain largely unexplored. This study developed and evaluated an explainable AI-based approach for hantavirus species identification using viral genome sequence fragments representing six hantavirus species. A transformer-based genomic representation approach (DNABERT-2) was used to generate representations for various Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models. Sequence redundancy was quantified before model development, and performance was assessed using a 99%-sequence-identity group-aware partitioning strategy with five-fold group-aware cross-validation and an independent internal test set. Direct sequence-similarity auditing confirmed that no sequence pair with ≥ 99% global nucleotide identity crossed the development and test boundary. LightGBM achieved the highest mean group-aware cross-validation performance, with an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.51%, Cohen’s Kappa coefficient of 99.41%, and Brier Score of 0.19%. On the independent internal test set, LightGBM achieved an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.25%. SHAP analysis identified influential nucleotide sequence tokens contributing to LightGBM predictions, while a separate DNABERT-2 attention-based analysis identified highly attended nucleotide sequence patterns within the genomic encoder. These findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed approach as an auxiliary method for post-sequencing hantavirus species identification, genomic surveillance, and sequence-based research.

source_records.abstract: Hantaviruses are important zoonotic pathogens associated with severe human diseases, including hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recognized the importance of strengthening hantavirus surveillance and early detection because of their public health impact. Nevertheless, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based approaches for hantavirus species identification from viral genome sequences remain largely unexplored. This study developed and evaluated an explainable AI-based approach for hantavirus species identification using viral genome sequence fragments representing six hantavirus species. A transformer-based genomic representation approach (DNABERT-2) was used to generate representations for various Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models. Sequence redundancy was quantified before model development, and performance was assessed using a 99%-sequence-identity group-aware partitioning strategy with five-fold group-aware cross-validation and an independent internal test set. Direct sequence-similarity auditing confirmed that no sequence pair with ≥ 99% global nucleotide identity crossed the development and test boundary. LightGBM achieved the highest mean group-aware cross-validation performance, with an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.51%, Cohen’s Kappa coefficient of 99.41%, and Brier Score of 0.19%. On the independent internal test set, LightGBM achieved an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.25%. SHAP analysis identified influential nucleotide sequence tokens contributing to LightGBM predictions, while a separate DNABERT-2 attention-based analysis identified highly attended nucleotide sequence patterns within the genomic encoder. These findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed approach as an auxiliary method for post-sequencing hantavirus species identification, genomic surveillance, and sequence-based research.

Article in Press Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75095-x Keywords Hantavirus · Species · Detection · Viral genome sequences · Explainable AI Introduction Hantaviruses are negative-sense, tri-segmented Ribonucleic Acid (RNA) viruses belonging to the family Hanta­ viridae1. They are zoonotic pathogens transmitted primarily to humans through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodent hosts1–3. More than 25 hantavirus species have been associated with human disease4, prin­ cipally causing two major clinical syndromes: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), predominantly associated with Old World hantaviruses, including Hantaan Orthohantavirus, Orthohantavirus Seoulense, Ortho­ hantavirus Puumalaense, and Orthohantavirus Dobravaense in Europe and Asia; and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), primarily associated with New World hantaviruses, including Sin Nombre Orthohantavirus and Orthohantavirus Andesense in the Americas4–6. Following an incubation period of approximately 2–4 weeks, both syndromes may initially present with a nonspecific febrile prodromal phase characterized by fever, myalgia, headache, and gastrointestinal symptoms, which can hinder early clinical recognition4,7. Treatment of hantavirus infection is primarily supportive because no widely approved specific antiviral ther­ apy is currently available. Timely recognition of infection may increase clinical awareness of potential complica­ tions and facilitate appropriate monitoring and supportive interventions. Post-mortem case reports have described patients who initially presented to emergency or primary care services with a nonspecific diagnosis of “viral syn­ drome”, without hantavirus infection being considered8–10. Progression to the cardiopulmonary phase of HCPS or the oliguric phase of HFRS is associated with an increased risk of severe complications, mortality, or persistent organ impairment8. Case fatality rates for HCPS can reach 30–50%, while HFRS accounts for tens of thousands of hospitalizations annually across Eurasia4. Disease severity may also differ among hantavirus species, further emphasizing the importance of accurate viral characterization4. Hantaviruses therefore remain important zoonotic pathogens of public health concern because of their potential for emergence, geographic expansion, and association with severe human disease11,12. The World Health Orga­ nization (WHO) has emphasized the importance of strengthening hantavirus surveillance, laboratory capacity, early detection, and outbreak response to reduce the public health impact of these infections13. Recent hantavirus events have further highlighted the need for timely epidemiological investigation, laboratory confirmation, and genomic characterization to support public health decision-making14. Accordingly, accurate characterization of circulating hantavirus species can contribute to genomic surveillance, investigation of viral diversity, and public health preparedness. Laboratory confirmation of hantavirus infection commonly relies on molecular and serological methods, including Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) and serological assays, such as Immu­ noglobulin M Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (IgM ELISA)15,16. Following molecular detection, spe­ cies-level characterization can provide additional information for investigating epidemiological patterns, viral diversity, disease-associated differences, and transmission dynamics relevant to public health surveillance17,18. Hantavirus species identification may be performed using species-specific molecular assays or genomic sequence analysis19,20. The increasing availability of viral sequence data therefore provides opportunities for computational approaches that can support post-sequencing species identification. Artificial Intelligence (AI), including Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), has increasingly been applied in medicine and healthcare data for tasks such as disease detection, diagnosis, and severity predic­ tion21–23. ML methods, such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), can model complex relationships within structured data and have been widely applied across clinical prediction tasks24–26. DL architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), have further expanded the ability to analyze high-dimensional Article in Press Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75095-x and sequential data21,27,28. More recently, transformer-based models pretrained on genomic sequences have pro­ vided an additional approach for generating contextual representations directly from nucleotide sequence data. Previous applications of AI to hantavirus research have predominantly focused on population-level outbreak or infection-risk prediction rather than species identification from viral nucleotide sequences29–31. For instance, Kazasidis et al. developed an SVM-based early-warning system for predicting annual Orthohantavirus Puuma­ laense outbreaks in Germany, achieving an accuracy of 82.8% using weather variables and beech flowering intensity29. Other computational studies have similarly examined associations among rodent population dynam­ ics, climatic variables, and human hantavirus case counts30,31. Clinical applications have also been investigated. Bulut and Klein developed Kantesti, a multilingual AI-assisted clinical decision-support system that analyzes routine blood-test results to estimate the risk of hantavirus infection32. Following deployment across 50,000 interpreted laboratory reports, the system identified three laboratory-confirmed hantavirus cases that had initially been misclassified by clinicians32. Nevertheless, these approaches address outbreak forecasting, infection-risk assessment, or detection rather than species identification from viral nucleotide sequences29–33. In contrast, AI-based analysis of viral nucleotide sequences has increasingly been investigated for other viruses. Rancati et al. developed DeepAutoCoV, an unsupervised deep autoencoder approach based on SARS- CoV-2 Spike sequences to identify emerging lineages and forecast those likely to become dominant, illustrating the potential of learned sequence representations for genomic surveillance34. Peng et al. developed ViraLM using a pretrained genome foundation model to identify viral sequences directly from nucleotide data, demonstrating the potential of foundation-model representations for viral sequence analysis35. More recently, Rancati et al. introduced SARITA, a generative language model trained on SARS-CoV-2 Spike S1 sequences that generated realistic sequences and reproduced evolutionary patterns associated with subsequently emerging variants36. Anal­ yses across European countries have also demonstrated associations between genomic sequencing activity and epidemiological indicators, further emphasizing the importance of sequence data within pathogen-surveillance frameworks37. Collectively, these studies illustrate the increasing use of AI and language-model-based sequence representations for viral identification, evolutionary analysis, lineage forecasting, and genomic surveillance; nev­ ertheless, corresponding applications to hantavirus species identification remain limited. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, no previous study has investigated AI-based hantavirus species identifi­ cation directly from viral nucleotide sequences while incorporating explainable AI (XAI) techniques for this task. Therefore, this study aimed to develop and evaluate multiple ML and DL models for post-sequencing hantavirus species identification using nucleotide sequence data and representations generated by a pretrained genomic transformer. XAI techniques were additionally incorporated to investigate sequence-level features contribut­ ing to model predictions and to provide complementary exploratory information regarding nucleotide sequence patterns emphasized by the genomic encoder. The proposed approach is intended for post-sequencing genomic analysis, surveillance, and research rather than for the initial diagnosis of hantavirus infection. The findings may contribute to future development of AI-assisted approaches for hantavirus species identification and sequence- based genomic investigation. Materials and methods Figure 1 presents the data-driven AI framework utilized in this study, encompassing dataset preparation, sequence preprocessing and representation generation, model development, performance evaluation, and explainability analysis. Dataset and data preprocessing The dataset comprised 2,571 hantavirus-positive patient-associated records with corresponding viral genome sequence fragments representing six hantavirus species38. The source dataset classified the positive records as Article in Press Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75095-x Bayou virus (Orthohantavirus Bayoui), Dobrava virus (Orthohantavirus dobravaense), Hantaan virus (Hantaan Orthohantavirus), Puumala virus (Orthohantavirus Puumalaense), Seoul virus (Orthohantavirus Seoulense), and Sin Nombre virus (Sin Nombre Orthohantavirus)1. The virus names provided in the source dataset were retained as species labels throughout this study. Each source record was associated with a dataset-specific identifier and one corresponding FASTA sequence record. The identifier consisted solely of a randomly assigned number used within the public dataset and did not correspond to an actual clinical or institutional patient identifier. No directly identifying patient information was available, and the accompanying patient-associated information was anonymous. The dataset included 426 Bayou, 427 Dobrava, 422 Hantaan, 431 Puumala, 435 Seoul, and 430 Sin Nombre records. The source documen­ tation did not provide a sequence-length distribution or specify whether the available viral sequences represented complete genomes, individual genomic segments, or partial sequence fragments. Hantavirus genomes comprise three RNA segments, designated small (S), medium (M), and large (L)1. Nev­ ertheless, the source dataset did not provide S-, M-, or L-segment annotations, genomic coordinates, original sequence-repository information, accession numbers, strain identifiers, or isolate identifiers. Consequently, the specific genomic segment and accession-level provenance of the analyzed sequences could not be determined from the available source information. Furthermore, the dataset did not provide independently verifiable links to the original clinical records or sequence repositories; therefore, the provenance of the patient-associated meta­ data and sequence records could not be independently verified beyond the information supplied with the public dataset38. The accompanying patient-level data included age, sex, geographic region, and sample date. Sample dates for the 2,571 positive records ranged from May 2024 to May 2026. The geographic variable represented the patient’s geographic region rather than the documented geographic origin of the viral sequence or isolate. These patient-level variables were used only for descriptive characterization and were not included as model inputs. The approximately balanced distribution of the six hantavirus classes reflected the composition of the positive records in the source dataset rather than a balancing or subsampling procedure performed in this study. The available source documentation does not indicate whether this distribution was deliberately imposed during construction of the original dataset; therefore, the class frequencies should not be interpreted as representing the natural epi­ demiological prevalence of the six hantavirus species. Before model development, sequence redundancy was systematically assessed to reduce the risk of sequence- level information leakage across evaluation partitions. Exact duplicate sequences were first identified by direct comparison of nucleotide strings. Among the 2,571 sequence records, 2,395 unique exact sequences were Fig. 1 Schematic overview of the proposed AI approach for hantavirus species identification. Article in Press Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75095-x identified. Forty-seven exact-duplicate groups comprised 223 records, corresponding to 176 redundant copies beyond one representative per group. No exact-duplicate group contained conflicting hantavirus species labels. Exact duplicates were retained because they represented distinct source records; nevertheless, identical sequences were constrained to remain within the same sequence-similarity group and, consequently, within the same data partition. Sequence-similarity clustering was subsequently performed using CD-HIT-EST39 at identity thresholds of 99%, 95%, and 90%. CD-HIT-EST was configured using global sequence identity with a minimum alignment coverage of 90% for both the shorter and longer sequences. Word sizes of 10, 10, and 8 were used for the 99%, 95%, and 90% thresholds, respectively. The 99% identity threshold was used to define near-identical sequence groups for the primary leakage-controlled partitioning strategy, whereas the 95% and 90% thresholds were evalu­ ated additionally to characterize broader sequence redundancy. Because the FASTA headers did not provide strain, isolate, accession, outbreak, or lineage identifiers suitable for grouping, the 99%-identity sequence clus­ ters were used as the grouping variable throughout development/test partitioning and cross-validation. Exact duplicates were therefore necessarily contained within the same 99%-identity cluster and could not occur across evaluation boundaries. Hantaviruses are negative-sense RNA viruses; nevertheless, the FASTA sequences were represented using the DNA-style nucleotide alphabet, with thymine (T) rather than uracil (U). Before tokenization, all 2,571 sequences were converted to uppercase and examined for noncanonical nucleotide characters, including N and the IUPAC ambiguity codes R, Y, S, W, K, M, B, D, H, and V, as well as U. Direct examination confirmed that all sequences contained only A, C, G, and T. Consequently, no ambiguous-nucleotide replacement, masking, imputation, sequence exclusion, or U-to-T conversion was required before tokenization. Sequence preprocessing and representation generation were performed using the transformer-based DNA­ BERT-2 model40 with the multimolecule/dnabert2 checkpoint. DNABERT-2 was selected as a general-purpose genome foundation model pretrained on multi-species genomic sequences, enabling evaluation of whether pre­ trained genomic representations could support hantavirus species identification without task-specific fine-tuning of the encoder. Previous comparative studies have demonstrated strong sequence-identification performance of DNABERT-2 across diverse genomic datasets, and genome foundation models have also been applied to viral sequence identification35,41. Each viral genome sequence fragment was tokenized using the corresponding DNABERT-2 tokenizer with a maximum input length of 512 tokens and right padding.
