papers.title: DEVELOPMENT OF A PCR TEST SYSTEM FOR THE GENETIC DIAGNOSIS OF HEMORRHAGIC FEVER WITH RENAL SYNDROME
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is an acute zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses. Reliable molecular diagnostics are essential for early detection and epizootiological surveillance. This study aimed to develop and validate a reverse transcription quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) assay for detection of HFRS-associated orthohantavirus RNA.Species-specific primers (HV P1-F and HV P1-R) and a TaqMan probe (HV P1) targeting the nucleocapsid protein (N) gene within the S segment were designed. A plasmid positive control containing a 242-bp target fragment was constructed. Analytical sensitivity, specificity, reproducibility, and repeatability were evaluated. Field testing included samples from 343 small mammals collected in endemic areas of the West Kazakhstan Region. The assay consistently detected the plasmid control from 1 ng/μL to 1 fg/μL, with Ct values of 37.35 and 37.73 at 1 fg/μL. No specific amplification was observed at 100 ag/μL. A strong linear relationship between Ct values and template concentration was obtained (R2 = 0.998). No false-positive reactions occurred with tick-borne encephalitis virus or Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus RNA. Reproducibility and repeatability showed 100% concordance of qualitative results. HFRS-associated orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 45 of 123 pooled field samples. The minimum infection prevalence was 13.1%, reaching 15.3% in Myodes glareolus and 13.3% in Apodemus uralensis and Microtus arvalis. The developed one-step RT-qPCR assay demonstrated high sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility and is suitable for routine diagnostics and surveillance of natural HFRS foci.

A strong linear relationship between Ct values and template concentration was obtained (R2 = 0.998). Keywords: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, RT-qPCR, molecular diagnosis, genetic diagnostics, primers, TaqMan probe, validation, hantavirus, orthohantavirus. INTRODUCTION Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains one of the most significant natural focal viral infections in Eurasia, causing tens of thousands of cases annually, partic- ularly in Asian and Eastern European countries [1–6]. Con- temporary climate change, anthropogenic transformation of ecosystems, rodent migration, and urbanization contribute to the expansion of reservoir species ranges, thereby increas- ing the risk of the emergence of new natural foci of the in- fection [7–10]. Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a viral zoonotic natural focal disease characterized by pronounced in- toxication, fever, specific vasculitis accompanied by hemor- rhagic manifestations, and the development of renal inflam- mation with damage to the renal tubules and interstitium, resulting in impaired renal filtration and disruption of fluid and electrolyte homeostasis [11]. HFRS is caused by ortho- hantaviruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae and genus Orthohantavirus [12]. Ortho hantaviruses exhibit consider- able ecological plasticity, a broad range of natural reservoir hosts, and complex patterns of circulation within small-mam- mal populations [13–15]. The genome of orthohantaviruses consists of three seg- ments of negative-sense single-stranded RNA: S, M, and L. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which binds viral RNA and participates in the formation of the ribo- nucleoprotein complex. N-gene sequences are widely used in the development of molecular assays for the detection of or- thohantaviruses [16–18]. In the Republic of Kazakhstan, official surveillance and registration of HFRS cases have been conducted since 2000, with 302 cases recorded during the period from 2000 to 2024. The disease occurs both as sporadic cases and outbreaks, with pronounced seasonality and a predominance among rural pop- ulations [17, 19–21]. The seasonal peak in hospitalizations oc- curs from November to January, accounting for up to 87.6% of cases, with the highest incidence observed in November. This pattern is associated with the mass migration of rodents into human dwellings and agricultural structures during the cold season. In natural foci, the pathogen is maintained pre- dominantly through circulation within rodent populations, in- cluding Microtus arvalis, Myodes glareolus, Apodemus ural- ensis, and other species [22, 23]. Conventional diagnostic methods for HFRS have substan- tial limitations. Classical virological investigations require propagation of the pathogen in specialized cell lines under BSL-3 containment conditions, which are available only in specialized virological laboratories. This process is labor-in- tensive and does not always yield successful results [24–26]. Serological methods may have insufficient specificity due to cross-reactivity with other orthohantaviruses and tick-borne pathogens and are also predominantly retrospective in nature. IgM antibodies against HFRS-associated viruses generally be- come detectable from 3–4 days after disease onset, whereas IgG antibodies typically appear by days 10–14 [11, 26–28]. In this context, RT-qPCR methods are considered a gold-standard approach for early diagnosis, providing high sensitivity, specificity, and rapid detection of viral RNA [29, 30]. International recommendations from the World Health 176 Eurasian Journal of Applied Biotechnology. No.3, 2026 DOI: 10.11134/btp.3.2026.18 Organization (WHO), the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the MIQE (Minimum In- formation for Publication of Quantitative Real-Time PCR Experiments) guidelines emphasize the need for validated RT-qPCR-based molecular platforms adapted to the genetic diversity and regional characteristics of circulating orthohan- tavirus strains [31–33]. Such approaches provide high ana- lytical sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility under the specific epidemiological and ecological conditions of indi- vidual natural foci. The closest analogue to the proposed test system is the “OM-HFRS-RV” assay (Registration Certificate No. РЗН 2021/15205, dated March 23, 2021, Russian Federation; “OM” product line developed by Syntol) for the detection of hantavirus RNA in biological specimens using real-time PCR. However, this assay has a limitation in that it requires a two- step reaction consisting of reverse transcription followed by amplification of the target RNA fragment. This increases the overall analysis time and reagent consumption [34]. The present study describes the design, development, and comprehensive validation of a novel one-step RT-qPCR test system for the molecular diagnosis of HFRS, including its ap- plication in field studies for the epizootiological surveillance of natural foci in Kazakhstan. The technical outcome of the study is the development of specific oligonucleotides, establishment of positive controls, and detection of HFRS-associated viral RNA using real-time reverse transcription PCR. MATERIALS AND METHODS Oligonucleotide Design and Synthesis An important step in the development of the PCR-based test system was the selection of an appropriate genetic tar- get. A fragment of the N gene located within the S segment of the negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome was se- lected as the target. The target region was selected based on a comparative analysis of S-segment sequences of HFRS-asso- ciated orthohantaviruses available in the GenBank/NCBI da- tabases, taking into account its suitability for primer and hy- drolysis probe design [16, 35]. During oligonucleotide design, multiple sequence align- ment of the N gene was performed. Sequence conservation within the proposed primer- and probe-binding regions, am- plicon length, melting temperatures (Tm), GC content, and the potential for secondary structure formation were evalu- ated. The design process followed the recommendations of the MIQE (Minimum Information for Publication of Quanti- tative Real-Time PCR Experiments) guidelines and aimed to minimize the risk of nonspecific amplification [33, 36, 37]. The specificity of the selected primer and probe sequences was assessed in silico using BLAST and Primer-BLAST by comparison against sequences available in the NCBI Gen- Bank database. Potential homology with non-target viral and bacterial genomes was also evaluated. The analysis revealed no significant sequence matches that could potentially result in nonspecific amplification of the target fragment. The self-complementarity of the oligonucleotides and the potential formation of hairpin structures, homodimers, and heterodimers were additionally assessed using OligoAnalyzer and AutoDimer software. Sequences with unfavorable pre- dicted characteristics were excluded from further experimen- tal evaluation [38, 39]. The following oligonucleotide sequences were selected for the detection of the N gene fragment within the S segment and are presented in Table 1. Oligonucleotide synthesis was performed at the National scientific center for especially dangerous infections (NSCEDI) using standard phosphoramidite chemistry on an H6 auto- mated DNA/RNA synthesizer (K&A Laborgeraete GbR, Ger- many). Phosphoramidites from Glen Research Corporation (USA) and reagents from emp BIOTECH (Germany) were used. Purification of the aqueous primer solutions from syn- thesis by-products was performed using Centri•Pure N10 col- umns (emp BIOTECH GmbH, Germany). The purified aqueous primer solutions were concentrated to dryness using a CentriVap concentrator (Labconco, USA) and subsequently resuspended in deionized water to a final concentration of 100 μM. Primer concentrations were deter- mined using a NanoPhotometer® P-300 spectrophotometer (Implen, Germany). The probes were synthesized by BIGL (Novosibirsk, Russia). The lyophilized probes were reconsti- tuted to a concentration of 100 μM. To assess the diagnostic performance of the assay based on the developed oligonucleotide system, a positive control was constructed using a recombinant plasmid containing the syn- thesized target fragment of the N gene from the S segment of an HFRS-associated orthohantavirus. The nucleotide sequence of the target insert is presented below: GATTGAAGATATTGAGTCACCATCATCGATAT- GGGTTTTTGCTGGAGCACCTGACCGTTGTCCAC- CAACATGCCTATTCATTGCAGGGATTGCTGAACTTG- GAGCATTCTTTTCTATCCTGCAGGACATGCGGAATA- CAATTATGGCCTCAAAGACAGTGGGAACATCT- GAAGAAAAGTTACGAAAGAAATCATCATTCTAT- CAGTCTTATCTCAGGCGAACACAATCAATGGGGA- TACAAC (242 bp). RT-qPCR optimization and amplification conditions RT-qPCR conditions were optimized using the plasmid positive control and a negative control containing deionized water instead of the template. The annealing temperature was determined empirically based on the intensity of the specific amplification signal and the absence of amplification in the negative control. No.3, 2026 DOI: 10.11134/btp.3.2026.18 RT-qPCR was performed using a Rotor-Gene 6000 re- al-time PCR cycler (Corbett Research, Australia), with fluo- rescence generated by the FAM reporter dye detected in the Green channel. The total reaction volume was 25 μL and con- sisted of 5.0 μL of 5× qPCR reaction mix, 1.0 μL of forward primer (20 pmol/μL), 1.0 μL of reverse primer (20 pmol/μL), 0.5 μL of probe (10 pmol/μL), 5.0 μL of sample RNA, and sterile deionized water to the final volume. The final concen- trations of the primers and probe were 0.8 μM and 0.2 μM, respectively. A run was considered valid when a typical sig- moidal amplification curve was observed for the positive con- trol and no increase in fluorescence signal was detected for the negative control. A sample was considered positive when the amplification curve crossed the predefined threshold within 45 cycles; in the absence of such a curve, the result was in- terpreted as negative. PCR validation To confirm the analytical performance characteristics of the developed reagent kit for the detection of HFRS-asso- ciated orthohantavirus RNA by reverse transcription quan- titative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR), a validation study was performed. The validation study was designed to assess the analytical sensitivity, analytical specificity, reproducibility, and repeatability of the assay. A preliminary assessment of the analytical sensitivity of the PCR component of the test system was performed using serial tenfold dilutions of the plasmid positive control in ac- cordance with established general approaches to the analyti- cal validation of molecular diagnostic methods [40, 41]. The lowest concentration consistently detected across replicates was determined, and the linearity of the relationship between Ct values and the logarithm of template concentration was as- sessed. A statistically validated limit of detection (LoD) for the complete RT-qPCR method was not established within the scope of the present study. Analytical specificity was evaluated using a panel of het- erologous viruses circulating in Kazakhstan, including tick- borne encephalitis virus and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fe- ver virus, in accordance with the requirements for differential diagnosis of natural focal infections. Interlaboratory testing was performed in three structural divisions of the NSCEDI: the Molecular Genetic Research Laboratory, the Laboratory of Natural Focal Viral Infections, and the OBTC-IL. Testing was conducted by different opera- tors on different days using Rotor-Gene 6000 and QuantStu- dio 5 real-time PCR instruments, as well as auxiliary reagents and consumables from different production lots. RNA extraction and field study design RNA was extracted from viral samples and field-mate- rial suspensions using the QIAamp RNA Mini Kit for 250 tests (QIAGEN, Germany), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The extracted RNA samples were subsequently used as templates to assess the specificity of the developed primer set. The field study employed an observational descriptive-an- alytical design. Small mammals were trapped in August–Sep- tember 2025 in HFRS-endemic districts of the West Kazakh- stan Region, including Burlinsky, Shyngyrlau, Terektinsky, and Baiterek districts. Trapping was performed using “Gero” traps baited with standard bread bait and placed at 2-m inter- vals. Species identification was based on morphological char- acteristics. Lung tissue samples were pooled by species and trapping location, resulting in 123 pooled samples derived from 343 individual animals. The minimum infection rate (MIR) was calculated as the number of positive pools divided by the total number of individuals tested and expressed as a percentage. The plasmid DNA concentration was determined us- ing the Quant-iT dsDNA HS Kit (Invitrogen, USA) on a Qu- bit fluorometer (Invitrogen, USA). Each concentration was tested in duplicate. Serial tenfold dilution of the positive plasmid control resulted in a consis- tent increase in Ct values in the Green/FAM channel. No.3, 2026 DOI: 10.11134/btp.3.2026.18 UDC:616.993 DEVELOPMENT OF A PCR TEST SYSTEM FOR THE GENETIC DIAGNOSIS OF HEMORRHAGIC FEVER WITH RENAL SYNDROME Rysbekova A.K.1, Zhumadilova Z.B. 1 , Yessimseit D.T. 1, Khaltayeva D.B. 1, Salavatov A.K. 1, Abdeliyev B.Z. 1, Abdirassilova A.A. 1, Tukhanova N.B. 1, Turebekov N.A. 1 , Umarova S.K. 1, Tokmurziyeva G.Zh. 1 , Iztleuov B.A. 2, Khakimov N.U.2 1 M. Aikimbayev National Scientific Center for Especially Dangerous Infections, 050054, Zhahanger st.,14, Almaty, Kazakhstan 2 Oral Anti-Plague Station, 090000, Chapayev st., 36/1, Oral, Kazakhstan *Corresponding author: salavatovalisher@gmail.com ABSTRACT Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is an acute zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses. Reliable mo- lecular diagnostics are essential for early detection and epizootiological surveillance. This study aimed to develop and vali- date a reverse transcription quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) assay for detection of HFRS-associated orthohantavirus RNA.Species-specific primers (HV P1-F and HV P1-R) and a TaqMan probe (HV P1) targeting the nucleocapsid protein (N) gene within the S segment were designed. A plasmid positive control containing a 242-bp target fragment was constructed. Analytical sensitivity, specificity, reproducibility, and repeatability were evaluated. Field testing included samples from 343 small mammals collected in endemic areas of the West Kazakhstan Region. The assay consistently detected the plasmid con- trol from 1 ng/μL to 1 fg/μL, with Ct values of 37.35 and 37.73 at 1 fg/μL. No specific amplification was observed at 100 ag/ μL. A strong linear relationship between Ct values and template concentration was obtained (R2 = 0.998). No false-positive reactions occurred with tick-borne encephalitis virus or Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus RNA. Reproducibility and repeatability showed 100% concordance of qualitative results. HFRS-associated orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 45 of 123 pooled field samples. The minimum infection prevalence was 13.1%, reaching 15.3% in Myodes glareolus and 13.3% in Apodemus uralensis and Microtus arvalis. The developed one-step RT-qPCR assay demonstrated high sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility and is suitable for routine diagnostics and surveillance of natural HFRS foci. Keywords: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, RT-qPCR, molecular diagnosis, genetic diagnostics, primers, TaqMan probe, validation, hantavirus, orthohantavirus. INTRODUCTION Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains one of the most significant natural focal viral infections in Eurasia, causing tens of thousands of cases annually, partic- ularly in Asian and Eastern European countries [1–6]. Con- temporary climate change, anthropogenic transformation of ecosystems, rodent migration, and urbanization contribute to the expansion of reservoir species ranges, thereby increas- ing the risk of the emergence of new natural foci of the in- fection [7–10]. Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a viral zoonotic natural focal disease characterized by pronounced in- toxication, fever, specific vasculitis accompanied by hemor- rhagic manifestations, and the development of renal inflam- mation with damage to the renal tubules and interstitium, resulting in impaired renal filtration and disruption of fluid and electrolyte homeostasis [11]. HFRS is caused by ortho- hantaviruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae and genus Orthohantavirus [12]. Ortho hantaviruses exhibit consider- able ecological plasticity, a broad range of natural reservoir hosts, and complex patterns of circulation within small-mam- mal populations [13–15]. The genome of orthohantaviruses consists of three seg- ments of negative-sense single-stranded RNA: S, M, and L. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which binds viral RNA and participates in the formation of the ribo- nucleoprotein complex. N-gene sequences are widely used in the development of molecular assays for the detection of or- thohantaviruses [16–18]. In the Republic of Kazakhstan, official surveillance and registration of HFRS cases have been conducted since 2000, with 302 cases recorded during the period from 2000 to 2024. The disease occurs both as sporadic cases and outbreaks, with pronounced seasonality and a predominance among rural pop- ulations [17, 19–21]. The seasonal peak in hospitalizations oc- curs from November to January, accounting for up to 87.6% of cases, with the highest incidence observed in November. This pattern is associated with the mass migration of rodents into human dwellings and agricultural structures during the cold season. In natural foci, the pathogen is maintained pre- dominantly through circulation within rodent populations, in- cluding Microtus arvalis, Myodes glareolus, Apodemus ural- ensis, and other species [22, 23]. Conventional diagnostic methods for HFRS have substan- tial limitations. Classical virological investigations require propagation of the pathogen in specialized cell lines under BSL-3 containment conditions, which are available only in specialized virological laboratories. This process is labor-in- tensive and does not always yield successful results [24–26]. Serological methods may have insufficient specificity due to cross-reactivity with other orthohantaviruses and tick-borne pathogens and are also predominantly retrospective in nature. IgM antibodies against HFRS-associated viruses generally be- come detectable from 3–4 days after disease onset, whereas IgG antibodies typically appear by days 10–14 [11, 26–28]. In this context, RT-qPCR methods are considered a gold-standard approach for early diagnosis, providing high sensitivity, specificity, and rapid detection of viral RNA [29, 30]. International recommendations from the World Health 176 Eurasian Journal of Applied Biotechnology. No.3, 2026 DOI: 10.11134/btp.3.2026.18 Organization (WHO), the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the MIQE (Minimum In- formation for Publication of Quantitative Real-Time PCR Experiments) guidelines emphasize the need for validated RT-qPCR-based molecular platforms adapted to the genetic diversity and regional characteristics of circulating orthohan- tavirus strains [31–33]. Such approaches provide high ana- lytical sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility under the specific epidemiological and ecological conditions of indi- vidual natural foci. The closest analogue to the proposed test system is the “OM-HFRS-RV” assay (Registration Certificate No. РЗН 2021/15205, dated March 23, 2021, Russian Federation; “OM” product line developed by Syntol) for the detection of hantavirus RNA in biological specimens using real-time PCR. However, this assay has a limitation in that it requires a two- step reaction consisting of reverse transcription followed by amplification of the target RNA fragment. This increases the overall analysis time and reagent consumption [34]. The present study describes the design, development, and comprehensive validation of a novel one-step RT-qPCR test system for the molecular diagnosis of HFRS, including its ap- plication in field studies for the epizootiological surveillance of natural foci in Kazakhstan. The technical outcome of the study is the development of specific oligonucleotides, establishment of positive controls, and detection of HFRS-associated viral RNA using real-time reverse transcription PCR. analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is an acute zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, requiring reliable molecular diagnostics for early detection and surveillance. papers.title: Host–Virus Immune Interactions in Andes Virus Infection: Implications for Human-to-Human Transmission, Pathogenesis, and Public Health
papers.abstract: The Andes virus (ANDV, Orthohantavirus, andesense) is unique among hantaviruses in that it may transfer from person to person and cause severe vascular damage. The evidence on host–virus immunological interactions and their importance in disease progression, transmission, and public health is compiled in this narrative review. ANDV mostly affects pulmonary endothelial cells and does not result in widespread cell loss. Rather, the loss of vascular barrier integrity is caused by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, Ras homolog family member A (RhoA) activation, breakdown of vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin, hypoxia-related pathways, and mediators produced from infected pericytes. Additionally, the virus interferes with early antiviral defenses involving protein kinase R (PKR), TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1)–interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS), and retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)/melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5). The intensity or outcome of the disease has been associated with increased interleukin-6 (IL-6), altered complement activity, thrombocytopenia, neutralizing-antibody reactions, and specific host genetic variations; nevertheless, significant T-cell activation does not necessarily correspond with viral clearance. Blood and a number of mucosal and secretory samples have been found to contain ANDV ribonucleic acid (RNA), albeit RNA discovery by itself does not prove the presence of an infectious virus. Epidemiological evidence indicates that Secondary transmission is rare and mostly linked to extended close or intimate contact. Genomic sequencing, when paired with epidemiological evidence, can shed light on transmission chains. Recent outbreaks linked to travel further emphasize the significance of worldwide surveillance and coordinated contact tracing. Prospective studies integrating genomic analysis, serial virological sampling, and standardized exposure evaluation are required to more effectively define the infectious phase and transmission patterns

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus known to transmit between humans and causes severe vascular damage.
analysis.main_directions: The review synthesizes host–virus immune interactions that drive disease progression, transmission, and public health implications.
analysis.current_state: ANDV infects pulmonary endothelial cells, disrupting vascular integrity through VEGF, RhoA, VE‑cadherin, hypoxia pathways, and pericyte‑derived mediators, while evading early antiviral signaling (PKR, TBK1–IRF3, MAVS, RIG‑I/MDA5). Severity associates with IL‑6, complement alterations, thrombocytopenia, neutralizing antibodies, and host genetics, yet T‑cell activation does not guarantee clearance.
analysis.gaps: RNA detection in blood and mucosal sites does not prove infectious virus; secondary transmission is rare and linked to close contact; genomic sequencing with epidemiology is required to trace chains, and travel‑related outbreaks expose surveillance gaps.
analysis.future_research: Prospective studies combining genomic analysis, serial virology, and standardized exposure evaluation are essential to delineate infectious phases and transmission dynamics.

papers.title_zh: 宿主–病毒免疫相互作用于 安第斯病毒 感染:对人际传播、发病机制及公共卫生的意义

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒(ANDV)是唯一已知能够在人与人之间传播的汉坦病毒,并导致严重的血管损伤。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述综合了宿主与病毒之间的免疫相互作用,这些相互作用驱动疾病进展、传播以及公共卫生影响。
analysis_zh.current_state: ANDV感染肺部内皮细胞,通过VEGF、RhoA、VE‐cadherin、缺氧通路以及周细胞来源的介质破坏血管完整性,同时逃避早期抗病毒信号通路(PKR、TBK1‐IRF3、MAVS、RIG‐I/MDA5)。疾病严重程度与IL‐6、补体改变、血小板减少、中和抗体以及宿主基因有关,但T细胞活化并不能保证清除。
analysis_zh.gaps: 血液和黏膜部位的RNA检测并不证明存在传染性病毒;二次传播罕见且与密切接触相关;需要结合流行病学的基因组测序来追踪传播链,旅行相关的暴发暴露了监测盲点。
analysis_zh.future_research: 前瞻性研究结合基因组分析、连续病毒学检测和标准化暴露评估,对于阐明传染阶段和传播动力学至关重要。

papers.title: Andes virus from the MV Hondius outbreak is highly pathogenic in hamsters and airborne shed
papers.abstract: In May 2026, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sparking public health measures in multiple countries. ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.

Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.

Soon after, ANDV was 49 diagnosed as the cause of the outbreak, which overall led to 13 reported cases, including three 50 deaths4. Confirmed cases were all aboard the MV Hondius, although the outbreak led to 51 monitoring of 653 individuals in 33 countries around the globe. 52 ANDV is classified within the family Orthohantaviridae5-8. These are viruses that cause two distinct 53 disease complexes: the hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe and Asia, and 54 the hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, caused among others by Sin Nombre 55 virus (SNV) and Andes virus (ANDV), respectively9. HPS is usually presents in four distinct clinical 56 phases: febrile, cardiopulmonary, diuretic and convalescent10,11. Most cases are characterized by 57 pulmonary edema driven by increased vascular permeability, terminally leading to cardiogenic 58 shock and death12. The case fatality rate of the MV Hondius outbreak was 23%, lower than for 59 previously reported ANDV clusters. Direct comparison is difficult however, due to the relatively 60 low number of cases in this outbreak and early access to medical care for many of the individuals 61 affected13-15. 62 ANDV is endemic in Southern Argentina and Chile, where it causes seasonal outbreaks every 63 year9,16. Humans are believed to become infected mostly after exposure to aerosolized infectious 64 excretions of the rodent reservoir, the long-tailed rice rat (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus)5,6,17. 65 Andes virus (ANDV) was first detected in 1995, when it caused an outbreak of 16 cases and nine 66 deaths18. This outbreak and subsequent ones suggested that ANDV can be capable of human- 67 to-human transmission, with the main risk factor being in close contact with infected individuals in 68 enclosed settings18,19. Some cases have also been described without any documented direct 69 contact, hinting at a respiratory transmission route, though available data cannot distinguish 70 airborne shedding of infectious virus from contamination of the surrounding environment20. On 71 the MV Hondius, patients were in direct contact with each other, suggesting ANDV human-to- 72 4 | P a g e human transmission. One potential asymptomatic case of ANDV infection in a health-care worker 73 with low-level viraemia was also reported, despite only indirect exposure21-23. 74 Few studies have phenotyped ANDV isolates obtained directly from human patients21-23, and 75 fewer still have done so in vivo to define key viral characteristics such as virulence and host 76 responses22,24. As a result, our understanding of the biological 79 differences between ANDV isolates associated with different cases and outbreaks is incomplete. 80 Here, we characterized the ANDV isolate associated with the MV Hondius outbreak 81 (ANDV/2026/hondius-NL-12, henceforth ANDV2026). Using the golden Syrian hamster model, we 82 studied viral pathogenesis, replication sites, and the host innate and adaptive immune responses. 83 We also analyzed virus shedding from infected animals and sampled air from the cages of infected 84 hamsters for ANDV RNA and infectious virus. Throughout our study, the human isolate ANDV2026 85 was compared with a rodent-derived ANDV strain (ANDV9717869). Altogether, in vivo phenotyping 86 contributes to the continuous risk assessment of emerging viruses of global health concern. 87 88 RESULTS 89 90 ANDV2026 causes severe, systemic infection in hamsters. Golden Syrian hamsters were 91 intranasally inoculated with a low dose (200 TCID50/hamster) of either ANDV2026 (n=18) or 92 ANDV9717869 (n=18). ANDV2026 was isolated from whole-blood sample collected from a pre- 93 symptomatic patient during the 2026 ANDV outbreak linked to the cruise ship MV Hondius3. 94 Backtitration of the inocula revealed that the animals received a dose of 28 TCID50 of ANDV2026 95 and 89 TCID50 of ANDV9717869. Six animals per group were sacrificed at 3, 7 and 14 days post- 96 inoculation (dpi), or earlier when reaching humane endpoints. Sixty percent of the hamsters 97 inoculated with ANDV2026 reached the humane endpoint between 12 and 14 dpi (Fig 1a). 98 5 | P a g e Symptoms included lethargy, ruffled fur, decreased mobility, and severe respiratory distress. In 99 general, animals reached humane endpoints within 24-72 hours after the onset of symptoms. The 100 development of clinical symptoms was also accompanied by a loss of body weight of up to 9% in 101 three days (Fig. 1b). At the terminal stage of the experiment (12-14 dpi), the lung-to-bodyweight 102 ratio of ANDV2026 inoculated animals was significantly increased when compared to both mock- 103 and ANDV9717869-inoculated animals (Fig. 1c). These values reflected the macroscopic lung 104 lesions observed in ANDV2026 inoculated animals, characterized by increased size, rounded edges 105 and darkened color with severe, diffuse lung oedema (Fig. 1d), as described previously for severe 106 ANDV infections in hamsters25-27. 107 Next, we tested 15 respiratory and non-respiratory tissues for presence of both viral RNA by qRT- 108 PCR and infectious virus by titration (Fig. 1e,f). At the early timepoints (3 dpi), viral RNA and 109 infectious virus were only detected in the nasal turbinates with titers essentially identical in both 110 ANDV2026- and ANDV9717869-inoculated animals. At 7 and 12-14 dpi all tissues contained both viral 111 RNA and infectious virus with titers in most cases higher in ANDV2026-infected animals. 112 Interestingly, we observed no significant differences in viral loads in myocardium and liver 113 between ANDV2026- and ANDV9717869-infected hamsters 12-14 dpi. These tissues were previously 114 reported as the prime targets of virus replication in ANDV9717869-infected hamsters26. We observed 115 the highest viral titers in the respiratory tract (nasal turbinates and lungs), submandibular salivary 116 glands, pancreas, and adrenal glands collected from ANDV2026-infected animals. 117 Sites of ANDV replication. Next, we investigated the sites of viral replication using 118 immunohistochemistry (IHC) and RNA in situ-hybridisation (ISH) in formalin-fixed and paraffin 119 embedded samples from inoculated animals. In the lungs, we detected abundant viral RNA (Fig. 120 2a) and protein in ANDV2026-infected animals at 7dpi, with widespread distribution in the 121 parenchyma. Quantification of RNA signal showed virus spread in wider areas of the lungs in 122 ANDV2026-infected hamsters compared to those infected with ANDV9717869 (Fig. 2b-c), both at 7 123 and 14 dpi. Virus RNA was detectable, both by qualitative assessment of the histological sections 124 6 | P a g e and by software-assisted image analysis28, in the lung parenchyma and endothelial cells, but not 125 in the bronchial epithelium of all ANDV infected animals at both 7 and 14 dpi (Fig. 2c-d). As 126 expected, extrarespiratory organs such as liver, kidney, myocardium, and many others showed 127 abundant viral RNA signal in endothelial cells, while epithelial cells were viral RNA negative (Fig. 128 2e). Importantly, we also detected ANDV2026 widely distributed in the brain, including in endothelial 129 cells of blood vessels, meninges and neurons (Fig. 2e and Fig. S1). 130 The widespread infection of endothelial cells throughout all organs was not accompanied by 131 severe histopathological lesions in both groups of animals. Serum chemistry revealed reduced 132 total protein and albumin concentrations in ANDV2026-infected hamsters compared to ANDV9717869- 133 and mock-infected animals, consistent with endothelial dysfunction and leakage of proteins to the 134 extravascular space (Fig. 2f). We found moderately abnormal values for alkaline phosphatase, 135 alanine-aminotransferase, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and phosphorus in ANDV2026-infected 136 animals (in the terminal stages of the disease), consistent with kidney and liver damage, although 137 major histopathological lesions were not observed (Fig. 2f, Fig. S2). Serum values of amylase, 138 calcium, glucose, sodium and total bilirubin remained similar between groups (Fig. S2). 139 Lung pathology in ANDV2026-infected hamsters correlates with preferential activation of the 140 type I IFN response. At the latest stages of disease, we detected histopathological lesions 141 throughout the lungs in hamsters infected with ANDV2026, similar to severe HPS previously 142 described in this model 25-27. Lesions include diffuse alveolar damage, multifocal, 143 lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, alveolar histiocytosis, alveolar oedema, leukocytolastic vasculitis, 144 perivascular oedema, sloughing of bronchial epithelial cells to various degrees and hemorrhages 145 in the vessel (Fig. 3a-b). We also detected fibrin accumulation in damaged alveoli in more severe 146 cases (Fig. 3b, middle panel). Infiltrates of both B-cells (Pax+ cells) and macrophage (Iba-1+ cells) 147 infiltrates, but not T-cells (CD3+), were observed in the lungs of ANDV2026-infected animals (Fig. 148 3c-d). 149 7 | P a g e In addition, activation of the type I IFN response (henceforth IFN), assessed by the upregulation 150 of the IFN-stimulated gene Mx-1, was evident in the lungs of both ANDV2026- and ANDV9217869- 151 infected animals (Fig. 3d, last column). We detected relatively little Mx-1 at 7 dpi despite the 152 presence of abundant virus replication. This observation reinforces the concept that ANDV is able 153 to evade recognition by the host IFN response for some time. 154 Because ANDV, both in humans and in hamsters, causes primarily a pulmonary disease, we 155 further investigated whether the levels of the IFN response vary between lungs and other organs 156 (Fig. 4). We found the highest relative expression of IFIT-1 RNA in the lungs, followed by 160 the spleen (Fig. 4). These data are in line with the relatively upregulation of proinflammatory 161 genes such as CXCL10 that we detected in these two organs (Fig. S3). At 7 dpi, antigen- 177 specific T-cell responses were limited in all groups (Fig. 5d). However, strong antigen-specific T- 178 cell responses were detected at 12-14 dpi regardless of group. The majority of virus-specific T- 179 cells targeted the L-protein (Fig. 5c, Fig. S4); these were comparable between ANDV9717869- and 180 ANDV2026-inoculated hamsters, and higher than those observed in mock-inoculated animals, 181 although significance was reached only for ANDV9717869 (Fig. 5e). N-specific T-cell responses 182 were higher in ANDV9717869-inoculated animals than in ANDV2026- and mock-inoculated animals at 183 12-14 dpi (Fig. 5e). Similar responses were observed with lymphocytes isolated from the spleen, 184 although the background in mock-inoculated hamsters was higher, complicating data 185 interpretation (Fig. S4). 186 Infectious virus is shed in the air by ANDV2026-infected animals. The ANDV outbreak aboard 187 the MV Hondius raised questions about the potential of increased shedding, and hence increased 188 transmissibility, of ANDV. In hamsters, we detected viral genomes (Fig. 6a) and infectious virus 189 (Fig. S5) in throat swabs of all ANDV2026-inoculated animals from 7 dpi onwards, with 190 progressively increasing titers until the end of the experiment (Fig. 6a). We detected infectious 191 virus in only one ANDV9717869-infected animal. By immunohistochemistry, we detected numerous 192 clusters of ANDV2026 infected endothelial cells, olfactory epithelium, degenerated and sloughing 193 olfactory epithelium, as well as the ducts of the nasal submucosal glands of the olfactory portion 194 of the turbinates, especially at 14 dpi. Only very few cells of the respiratory epithelium showed 195 occasionally virus positive signal (Fig. 6d-f). ANDV9717869-inoculated animals displayed only 196 occasional virus-positive cells in the nasal turbinates (either endothelial cells, cells within the 197 olfactory epithelium, or the submucosal glands). 198 We also detected ANDV2026 RNA in urine collected at study endpoints, but volumes were too small 199 to test for presence of infectious virus. papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒 来自 MV Hondius 爆发的病毒在仓鼠中高度致病并通过空气排出

analysis_zh.background: 在2026年5月,检测到在邮轮 MV Hondius 上爆发的 汉坦病毒肺综合征(汉坦病毒肺综合征),其病原为 安第斯病毒(安第斯病毒),凸显了人际传播的动物源病毒的公共卫生影响。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究使用来自无症状患者的安第斯病毒分离株感染金叙利亚仓鼠,评估致病机制、病毒复制部位、先天和适应性免疫应答以及病毒排泄,并以鼠源安第斯病毒分离株作为对照。
analysis_zh.results: ANDV2026 在仓鼠中高度致病,引起严重肺部疾病,I型干扰素和炎症反应延迟,在呼吸道及呼吸道外组织(包括脑)复制,诱导中和抗体和 T 细胞应答,并通过多种途径排出传染性病毒,包括可检测的空气传播病毒;对照仓鼠的病毒排泄量很少。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现巩固了已知的安第斯病毒致病特征,同时揭示了空气排泄等新特性,强调对患者来源分离株进行表型表征以备疫情防控和对策研发的价值。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未在提供的证据中报告。

papers.title: Design and in silico evaluation of PV-GNProtecta: an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis.
papers.abstract: Abstract Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli -based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection.

PUUV infection commonly presents with sudden fever, head- ache, back pain, nausea, gastrointestinal symptoms, thrombocytopenia, hematuria, and varying degrees of acute kidney impairment [1, 8]. In some patients, addi- tional manifestations such as blurred vision, dizziness, insomnia, respiratory complications, oliguria, and sub- sequent polyuria during recovery may also occur [2, 9]. Although PUUV infection is generally considered mild, severe complications can occur in a subset of patients, including acute kidney failure, hypotension, shock, pul- monary edema, Guillain-Barré syndrome, respiratory distress, disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC), myocarditis, encephalitis, pituitary hemorrhage, seizures, and, in rare cases, multiorgan failure or fatal cerebral hemorrhage [2, 3, 10, 11]. The first identification of PUUV occurred in the early 1980s when the virus was isolated from bank voles (Myodes glareolus) in the Puumala region of Finland [2]. Between July 1989 and June 1996, Finland reported 6701 PUUV infection cases confirmed via serologi- cal assays, with the highest incidence in the Itä-Savo district and a mortality rate below 0.1%, and later from 1995 to 2008, 22,681 cases were recorded with an average annual incidence of 31 per 100,000 population, resulting in 13 deaths and 52% of patients requiring hospitaliza- tion [12, 13]. PUUV accounts for approximately 93% of all notified hantavirus infections in Germany and caused a major outbreak in 2007 in Baden-Württemberg with 1089 reported human cases, while the highest annual number of PUUV infections in Germany was recorded in 2010 since hantavirus surveillance began in 2001 [14, 15]. Also in 2007, Sweden’s Västerbotten County experi- enced a surprisingly severe outbreak of PUUV infection, with NE rates hitting 313 cases per 100,000 residents [16, 17]. Between 2001 and 2017, a total of 12,148 hantavirus disease cases were recorded, of which 9714 (approxi- mately 97.41%) were attributed to PUUV infection [18]. In 2019, Europe recorded over 4000 hantavirus cases (0.8 per 100,000), 98% caused by PUUV, with Finland and Germany making up 69% of the total [19]. From 2018 to 2025, Hungary recorded 51 lab-confirmed hantavirus infections, 20 of which were specifically linked to the PUUV [20]. In Finland, between 560 and 3800 cases of NE are reported each year, though the actual number is believed to be nearly six times higher [21]. PUUV is a spherical enveloped pathogen character- ized by a segmented negative-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome [5, 21]. The PUUV possesses a tripartite genome: the L segment (~ 6.5 kb) encodes a ~ 2156-amino-acid L protein (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) with replicase, transcriptase, and endo- nuclease functions; the M segment (~ 3.7 kb) encodes a ~ 1148-amino-acid glycoprotein precursor that is co- translationally cleaved into Gn (70 kDa) and Gc (55 kDa); and the S segment (~ 1.8 kb) encodes a ~ 433-amino-acid nucleocapsid (N) protein [2, 5, 22, 23]. Gc is the protein that mediates fusion by the identification of a peptide of fusion, whereas Gn serves as a folding chaperone for Gc and controls the time of fusion; both are necessary for the virus to adhere as well as enter host cells [2, 24]. Gn and Gc form the principal antigenic surface of PUUV and are major targets of neutralizing antibodies, contributing to protective immunity and vaccine relevance [25–27]. The N protein plays multiple roles in viral genome transport, replication, and assembly through its interactions with host cellular proteins, while also acting as a highly immu- nogenic viral component in both humans and animal models [28, 29]. The N protein is highly conserved among orthohantaviruses and elicits a strong early antibody response during acute infection, making it an important target for both diagnostic applications and vaccine devel- opment [30, 31]. Various vaccine platforms are available, each possess- ing distinct advantages and drawbacks. For example, live attenuated vaccines trigger strong, long-lasting immu- nity but can be risky for immunocompromised individu- als due to possible reversion to virulence; inactivated vaccines are safer and more stable, though they usually require multiple doses; subunit vaccines use only key antigens, lowering the chance of side effects, but often need adjuvants and booster shots to achieve durable pro- tection [32–35]. Moreover, DNA vaccines offer rapid, stable, and cost-effective production with long-lasting immunity, but they often show weak immunogenicity in humans and face delivery challenges [34, 36]. In con- trast, the key advantage of mRNA vaccines lies in their rapid design and production, enabling swift responses to emerging infections and pandemic threats without the need to culture live pathogens [37, 38]. In recognition of these advances, the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine honored Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman Page 3 of 26 Hossain et al. Genomics & Informatics (2026) 24:19 for their groundbreaking contributions to nucleoside engineering, a key innovation that enabled the successful development of mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 [39]. Recent developments in bioinformatics have improved biopharmaceutical design by enabling rapid prediction of protein features, structural modeling, and immuno- genicity assessment. These computational approaches accelerate the identification and optimization of thera- peutic candidates while reducing time and experimental costs; however, challenges related to prediction accuracy, biological complexity, and the need for experimental validation remain important considerations [40]. Reverse vaccinology (RV) applies bioinformatics and immuno- informatics to screen microbial genomes for conserved, immunogenic epitopes, enabling faster, safer, and cost- effective vaccine development compared to traditional pathogen culturing, a slow and labor-intensive process [41, 42]. Vaccine development against PUUV infection has included inactivated whole-virus vaccines, recom- binant subunit vaccines, virus-like particle (VLP)-based approaches, and DNA vaccines [43–45]. Among these, inactivated and DNA vaccine candidates have demon- strated promising immunogenicity in preclinical studies [44–46]. Currently, no vaccine has been authorized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for PUUV infection [9, 47]. Several studies have suggested the potential of multi- epitope vaccine approaches using immunoinformatics- based strategies. Khan et al. developed a multi-epitope vaccine candidate against SARS-CoV-2 by integrating epitope prediction, antigenicity assessment, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response analysis, demonstrating the feasibility of com- putational vaccine design approaches [48]. Similarly, Peele et al. designed a multi-epitope vaccine construct containing predicted B-cell and T-cell epitopes and evaluated its structural and immunological proper- ties through computational analyses [49]. These studies highlighted the potential of combining multiple immune targets within a single vaccine construct; however, their findings remained primarily dependent on computa- tional predictions and required experimental validation to confirm immunogenicity and protective efficacy. However, despite these advances, several challenges remain in current multi-epitope vaccine development strategies. Computational vaccine designs are depend- ent on prediction algorithms, reference databases, structural modeling assumptions, and available biologi- cal information, which may influence the reliability of predicted vaccine candidates. In addition, variations in epitope selection criteria, antigen conservation analysis, population coverage evaluation, and structural validation approaches can affect the effectiveness of computational vaccine design. Recent studies have emphasized that although immunoinformatics approaches accelerate multi-epitope vaccine development, comprehensive experimental validation remains essential for confirming biological relevance and protective potential [50]. Despite previous vaccine development efforts, includ- ing inactivated whole-virus vaccines, recombinant subu- nit vaccines, virus-like particle (VLP)-based approaches, and DNA vaccine candidates, no PUUV vaccine has currently received regulatory approval. An integrated mRNA multi-epitope vaccine strategy targeting con- served regions of both PUUV glycoproteins (Gn/Gc) and nucleocapsid protein remains insufficiently explored. A comprehensive framework combining conserved antigen identification, multi-epitope vaccine construction, struc- tural evaluation, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response prediction for PUUV has not been extensively investigated. Therefore, this study aimed to design and evaluate the PV-GNProtecta vaccine candidate using an integrated immunoinfor- matics workflow involving conserved antigen identifica- tion, epitope prediction, structural modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response prediction. The findings provide computational insights into the potential characteristics of PV-GNPro- tecta while recognizing the necessity of experimental val- idation for future assessment. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Acquisition and characterization of viral protein sequences The UniProt protein database (https://​www.​unipr​ot.​org/; accessed on 15 July 2025) was used for obtaining amino acid sequences of the target proteins from PUUV of G (accession number: P41266) and N (accession numbers: P41270) [51]. The G and N proteins were selected due to their key roles in PUUV infection and immune recogni- tion. The G protein mediates viral attachment and entry and is a major target of neutralizing antibodies, whereas the highly conserved N protein contributes to viral repli- cation and induces strong immune responses. Compared with the intracellular RdRp/L protein, G and N provide more suitable targets for antibody and cellular immune responses. A comparative evaluation of these proteins is provided in Supplementary Table S14. 2.2 Physicochemical and structural characterization of selected proteins The selected PUUV G and N proteins were character- ized for signal peptide presence, transmembrane regions, and subcellular localization. Signal peptide predic- tion was performed using SignalP 6.0 (https://​servi​ces.​ healt​htech.​dtu.​dk/​servi​ces/​Signa​lP-6.​0/; accessed on 15 Page 4 of 26 Hossain et al. Genomics & Informatics (2026) 24:19 September 2026) with the organism group selected as Eukarya and the default prediction model [52]. Trans- membrane topology was predicted using DeepTMHMM version 1.0.57 (accessed on 15 September 2026) using the default settings [53]. Subcellular localization informa- tion was obtained from UniProt (https://​www.​unipr​ot.​ org/; accessed on 15 September 2026) based on available curated annotations [54]. 2.3 Analysis of multiple sequence alignment and evolutionary relationships To support RV analysis, the sequence is encoded using amino acid residue codes and preserved as a FASTA sequence file. The acquired sequences were subsequently utilized for multiple sequence alignment (MSA) through the Clustal Omega platform (https://​www.​ebi.​ac.​uk/​ jdisp​atcher/​msa/​clust​alo; accessed on 05 August 2025) [55]. The Mega X tool (https://​www.​megas​oftwa​re.​net/; accessed on 05 August 2025) was employed for phyloge- netic analysis on both genomes [56]. 2.4 Prediction of epitopes for MHC I, MHC II, and linear B‐cell interactions The MHC I epitopes from the G and N proteins were found using the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) (http://​tools.​iedb.​org/​mhci/; accessed on 20 August 2025) software, with a percentile rank < 1.00 as the selec- tion criterion [57]. This tool is a sophisticated database comprising information on MHC molecules, T-cell and B-cell epitopes, antibodies, and MHC-binding ligands identified in humans and various animal taxonomic groups, including primates and rodents [58, 59]. A cut- off percentile rank of less than 1.00 was implemented for epitope selection, which suggests that the binding affinity was improved [37]. Lower percentile rank values indicate stronger predicted peptide–MHC binding affin- ity [60]. The IEDB (http://​tools.​iedb.​org/​mhcii/; accessed on 20 August 2025) was applied to forecast the MHC II epitopes inside the designated areas of these proteins, and peptides with percentile ranks < 1.00 were considered potential high-affinity binders and selected for further evaluation [61]. Subsequently, the human allele reference sets were employed to predict CD8 + and CD4 + bind- ing. The ABCpred tool (https://​webs.​iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​ va/​abcpr​ed/; accessed on 25 August 2025) was used to estimate the continuous B-cell epitopes of the selected portions of these proteins. This tool provides epitope predictions by analyzing the sequence features of the tar- get antigens [58, 62]. This program uses an affinity scale method based on a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to predict continuous B-cell epitopes [63, 64]. Additionally, the MHC-II epitopes underwent some additional analy- ses, including IL-10 (https://​webs.​iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​va/​ il10p​red/; accessed on 25 September 2026), IFN-gamma (https://​webs.​iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​va/​ifnep​itope/​predi​ct.​ php; accessed on 25 September 2026), IL-2 (https://​webs.​ iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​va/​il2pr​ed/; accessed on 25 September 2026) and IL-4 (https://​webs.​iiitd.​edu.​in/​ragha​va/​il4pr​ ed/​design.​php; accessed on 25 September 2026) by using the respective servers. Genomics & Informatics Design and in silico evaluation of PV‐GNProtecta: an mRNA multi‐epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis Tanvir Hossain1, Abdullah Al Mahmud1, Maisha Afrin2, Sakibur Rahman1, Shaheda Siddiqa Tahia1, Ahmad Abdullah Mahdeen3* and Md. Habib Ullah Masum4* Abstract Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population cov- erage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escheri- chia coli-based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection. papers.title: Framing the 2026 Global Hantavirus Outbreak in Nigerian Online Newspapers: Insights from Premium Times and Sahara Reporters
papers.abstract: Background: Emerging infectious diseases often attract significant media attention because of their potential impact on public health perceptions and preparedness. Despite the absence of confirmed cases in Nigeria, the 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak generated global public health concern because of increased international mobility and the potential risk of cross-border transmission. Objective: This study investigated how Premium Times and Sahara Reporters framed the 2026 global hantavirus outbreak, focusing on the frequency, presentation formats, prominence, and dominant frames of coverage. Method: The study employed a content analysis design. Using census approach, all hantavirus-related stories published by Premium Times and Sahara Reporters between 2 and 30 May 2026 were identified, yielding 29 stories for analysis. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, while Holsti’s (1969) formula was used to assess inter-coder reliability, yielding a reliability coefficient of 0.85. Results: Premium Times published 17 stories (58.6%), while Sahara Reporters published 12 stories (41.4%). Of the 29 stories, 24 (82.8%) were news stories, 19 (65.5%) received low prominence, and 10 (34.5%) adopted a health risk/awareness frame, followed by the prevention and safety measures frame (5 stories; 17.2%) and the attribution of responsibility frame (4 stories; 13.8%). Conclusion: Nigerian online newspapers reported the outbreak primarily as a public health risk but devoted limited attention and prominence to the issue, suggesting a predominantly reactive orientation in the newspapers' reporting of emerging health threats. Unique Contribution: This study contributes empirical evidence on Nigerian media framing of the 2026 global hantavirus outbreak and extends health communication scholarship on emerging zoonotic diseases. Key Recommendation: Nigerian online newspapers should adopt more sustained, prominent, explanatory, and interpretative reporting of emerging infectious diseases to strengthen public preparedness and risk communication.
authors: Valentine Okwudilichukwu Ezema, Sunday Uche Aja, Mercy Ifeyinwa Obichili, Joseph N. Chukwu, Chika Thonia Ezeali, Ijeoma Njideka Taiwo & Kelvin Chinemerem Nkwuda

analysis_zh.limitations: 本分析仅限于两家线上报纸和短时间窗口;编码员间信度为中等(0.85);摘要未报告样本量细节或更广泛的背景因素。

papers.title: Hantavirus Outbreak on MV Hondius Cruise Ship: India’s Port Health Preparedness – A One Health Perspective
papers.abstract: Abstract The MV Hondius outbreak, reported in May 2026, is among the first large multinational hantavirus clusters linked to cruise ship travel. By July 2, 2026, when the outbreak was declared over, 13 cases (12 laboratory-confirmed and one probable) and three deaths had been reported, with contact tracing involving 33 countries and territories; no confirmed cases were reported in India. The identified Andes virus strain is notable for limited person-to-person transmission. This viewpoint is an interpretation of the outbreak using publicly available reports, scientific literature, and official communications from health agencies within a One Health framework, focusing on implications for India’s port health preparedness. The outbreak highlights how ecological exposure, international mobility, and a confined maritime environment can facilitate disease spread. India’s port health infrastructure includes pre-arrival vessel risk assessment, passenger thermal scanning, and contingency plans aligned with the International Health Regulations (IHR) 2005. Although hantavirus strains identified in India are not associated with person-to-person transmission, existing seroprevalence data support the need for continued surveillance. Strengthening a One Health approach integrating human, animal, and environmental surveillance is essential for future maritime outbreak preparedness. Trained port health personnel, improved diagnostics, and effective public communication remain essential.

By July 2, 2026, when the outbreak was declared over, 13 cases (12 laboratory-confirmed and one probable) and three deaths had been reported, with contact tracing involving 33 countries and territories; no confirmed cases were reported in India. The identified Andes virus strain is notable for limited person-to-person transmission. This viewpoint is an interpretation of the outbreak using publicly available reports, scientific literature, and official communications from health agencies within a One Health framework, focusing on implications for India’s port health preparedness. papers.title: Rising spillover risk: Lessons from the Andes hantavirus outbreak
papers.abstract: The unprecedented expansion of human activity boundaries is turning spillover from a chance event into a foreseeable ecological and epidemiological certainty. Using the 2026 Andes hantavirus cruise ship outbreak as an entry point, this study examines it within a broader driver framework: nearly all emerging infectious disease events in humans in recent decades have originated from wildlife transmission; under climate-change and land-use scenarios, approximately 3139 mammal species are projected to aggregate in new combinations by 2070, causing an estimated 4000 cross-species viral transmission events. The rapid expansion of tourism into ecologically fragile regions — sub-Antarctic waters, the deep sea, and primary forests — the persistence of habitat fragmentation and animal trade, and the reshaping of wildlife distribution and vector dynamics by extreme climate events together constitute “novel contact amplifiers” that accelerate contact at the human–animal–environment interface. Robotics, artificial intelligence, autonomous driving, and automated logistics are extending human activities into previously inaccessible regions, yet they remain almost entirely absent from current spillover risk assessments. The limitations of cruise ship medical systems — whose core capacity lies in “recognize, isolate, stabilize, and transfer” rather than definitive diagnosis and treatment — were fully exposed in this event. From a One Health perspective, this paper proposes that responses to spillover risk must shift from passive reaction to proactive interface governance, incorporate technology-driven increases in contact frequency into prevention and control frameworks, and advance cornerstone strategies such as broad-spectrum vaccines and broad-spectrum antiviral drugs at the basic research level.

papers.title_zh: 上升的溢出风险:安第斯病毒 汉坦病毒 疫情的经验教训

analysis_zh.background: 人类活动范围的扩展正将跨种传播从偶然事件转变为可预见的生态和流行病学必然,且几乎所有近期人类新发传染病事件均源自野生动物传播 (A1, A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究以2026年安第斯病毒 汉坦病毒 邮轮暴发为切入点,并在更广泛的野生动物来源新发驱动因素框架下进行分析 (A2)。
analysis_zh.results: 在气候变化和土地利用情景下,预计到2070年约有3,139种哺乳动物将以新组合聚集,进而导致约4,000起跨种病毒传播事件 (A3)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本文指出旅游、栖息地碎片化、动物贸易及其他“新型接触放大器”加速了人畜接触,并提出主动的One Health治理以及研发广谱疫苗和抗病毒药物的建议 (A4, A7)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅基于摘要,未报告详细的暴发数据、方法和定量验证;机器人、人工智能及其他新兴技术对跨种传播风险评估的影响亦未涉及 (A5, A6)。

papers.title: Human febrile illness associated with Yanggou tick virus: Clinical characteristics and epidemiological links to rodents.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: We identified Yanggou tick virus (YGTV), a segmented flavivirus previously unrecognized as a human pathogen, in a patient presenting with fever and headache. This study aims to characterize the epidemiology and clinical manifestations of YGTV infection in patients with fever of unknown origin (FUO). METHODS: We conducted a surveillance study at the First Hospital of Jilin University (2020-2025) involving 1,011 patients with FUO. Concurrently, ticks and rodents in the vicinity of the patients' residences and workplaces were collected for viral detection. YGTV infection was confirmed via PCR assays. Positive samples were used for viral isolation, genome amplification, and phylogenetic characterization. An Apodemus agrarius challenge model was established to evaluate viral persistence and shedding. RESULTS: Of the 30 confirmed cases of YGTV infection, 10 were co-diagnosed with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). The patients showed no clear seasonality or geographic bias. Notably, rodent contact (43.3%) was a more frequent risk factor than tick bites (6.7%). While clinical presentations were non-specific, nearly 50% of the patients presented with gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms. YGTV was isolated from patients, ticks, and A. agrarius (the latter often co-infected with Hantaan virus). Animal models confirmed persistent splenic infection and viral shedding via oral and fecal routes. CONCLUSION: Our findings establish YGTV as an underdiagnosed cause of human febrile illness, underscoring the transmission risks posed by tick vectors and rodent reservoirs. These results highlight the urgent need for enhanced clinical surveillance and diagnostic screening among patients presenting with FUO, particularly in regions where the virus is endemic.

analysis.summary_en: Background: YGTV, a segmented flavivirus, had not been recognized as a human pathogen (A1). Methods: A surveillance study (2020‑2025) of 1,011 FUO patients collected ticks and rodents, confirmed YGTV by PCR, performed viral isolation and phylogenetics, and used an Apodemus agrarius model (A3‑A7). Results: Thirty cases were confirmed, ten co‑diagnosed with HFRS; no seasonality/geographic bias, rodent contact (43.3%) exceeded tick bites (6.7%); ~50% had GI or neurological symptoms; virus isolated from patients, ticks, and rodents; animal models showed persistent splenic infection and oral/fecal shedding (A8‑A14). papers.title_zh: 与羊沟蜱病毒相关的人类发热疾病:临床特征及与啮齿动物的流行病学关联

analysis_zh.background: 羊沟蜱病毒(YGTV)是一种分段黄病毒,之前未被认定为人类病原体(A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 一项监测研究(2020‐2025)在吉林大学第一医院纳入了1,011例不明原因发热患者(A3)。在患者居住和工作场所附近采集蜱和啮齿动物(A4),并通过PCR确认YGTV感染(A5);阳性样本进行分离、基因组扩增和系统发育分析(A6)。采用田野鼠(Apodemus agrarius)挑战模型评估病毒的持续感染和排泄(A7)。
analysis_zh.results: 共鉴定出30例YGTV阳性病例,其中10例合并诊断为肾综合征出血热(A8)。病例未表现出明显的季节性或地域偏好(A9),且啮齿动物接触率(43.3%)高于蜱叮咬率(6.7%)(A10)。约50%的患者出现胃肠或神经系统症状(A11)。YGTV已从患者、蜱和田野鼠中分离(A12‐A13),动物模型显示脾脏持续感染并通过口腔和粪便排泄(A14)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究确认YGTV是人类发热疾病的未被充分诊断的致病因素,并强调蜱和啮齿动物储存宿主的传播风险(A15)。它凸显了在流行地区加强临床监测和对不明原因发热(FUO)进行诊断筛查的必要性(A16)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供了摘要;未报告详细的方法学、统计分析及更广泛的流行病学背景。

papers.title: Fractional optimal control of hantavirus transmission between rodents and humans
papers.abstract: This paper studies a fractional optimal control problem for a hantavirus transmission model involving interactions between rodent reservoirs and human populations. The model is formulated through a modified SIR–SIR structure, where both humans and rodents are divided into susceptible, infected, and recovered classes. The classical integer-order model is extended by using the Caputo fractional derivative, which captures memory and hereditary effects in the disease dynamics. Three time-dependent control variables are introduced: rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans. Positivity, boundedness, existence, and uniqueness of solutions are established to guarantee the biological and mathematical validity of the model. An optimal control problem is then formulated to minimize infected humans, infected rodents, and the costs of intervention. Necessary optimality conditions are derived using Pontryagin’s maximum principle for fractional systems. The adjoint equations, transversality conditions, and explicit characterization of the optimal controls are obtained. A numerical scheme based on the fractional Adams–Bashforth–Moulton predictor–corrector method combined with the forward–backward sweep algorithm is implemented. Several numerical scenarios are investigated, including no control, single-control strategies, and combined optimal controls. The simulations show that the combined strategy gives the strongest reduction in both infected humans and infected rodents. The results illustrate how memory-dependent dynamics can alter the predicted transmission trajectories and optimal intervention profiles. However, empirical calibration and validation using compatible human and rodent surveillance data are required before the model can be used for outbreak-specific prediction.
