Keywords Hantavirus transmission, Fractional optimal control, Caputo derivative, Pontryagin maximum principle, Fractional epidemic systems, Forward–backward sweep method Hantavirus infection is a serious zoonotic disease transmitted mainly through infected rodents and contaminated environmental materials such as urine, saliva, and feces1–3. The disease represents an important global public health challenge because of its high mortality rates, rapid respiratory complications, and increasing geographical spread4–6. Several strains of hantaviruses have been identified worldwide, including strains responsible for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome7–9. Human infection generally occurs through inhalation of aerosolized particles from infected rodents, although evidence of human-to- human transmission has also been reported in specific outbreaks10 (Fig. 1). Rodents are considered the principal reservoirs of hantaviruses12,13. Long-term epidemiological studies confirmed that environmental conditions, climate fluctuations, rodent migration, and habitat changes play significant roles in the persistence and transmission of hantavirus infection14–18. In Asia and South America, several investigations revealed increasing prevalence rates associated with ecological changes and urbanization5,9,19. In Indonesia, hantavirus infections have attracted increasing scientific interest due to the existence of infected rodent reservoirs in several provinces20–22. Mathematical modeling has become an essential tool for understanding the spread and control of infectious diseases23–26. Classical epidemic models based on ordinary differential equations have been successfully applied to many zoonotic diseases27,28. Several mathematical models for hantavirus transmission have been developed in the literature. Abramson and Kenkre studied spatial and spatiotemporal patterns in hantavirus spread14,15. Allen et al. proposed deterministic and ecological models describing rodent-host interactions and environmental variability29–31. Wesley et al. analyzed direct and indirect transmission mechanisms in rodent Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:31685 2 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-72549-0 www.nature.com/scientificreports populations32. Additional modeling investigations involving ecological risk mapping, stochastic fluctuations, and environmental effects were developed in33–35. Although classical integer-order models provide useful qualitative insights, they often fail to capture memory and hereditary effects observed in biological systems. Many infectious diseases exhibit nonlocal temporal dynamics in which the future state depends not only on the present state but also on the history of the system. Fractional calculus provides a powerful mathematical framework for incorporating these memory effects into epidemiological models36–38. Fractional-order epidemic models have shown improved accuracy in describing long-memory biological processes and nonlinear transmission dynamics39. Biological justification for the Caputo derivative The use of the Caputo fractional derivative is motivated by biological and epidemiological processes that depend on accumulated history rather than only on the current state. Hantavirus risk is influenced by prior rodent abundance, repeated or prolonged contact with contaminated excreta, persistence of infectious material in the environment, delayed effects of habitat and climate variation, and time-distributed host recovery and immune responses. These mechanisms introduce temporal dependence that may not be represented adequately by a local first-order derivative. The Caputo operator describes such effects through a power-law memory kernel, so recent and earlier epidemic states contribute with different weights to the present rate of change. It is also suitable for population models because it permits conventional initial conditions expressed directly through the initial compartment sizes. The fractional order inline-eq-IEq1 is therefore interpreted as a phenomenological memory parameter. The value in l ine-eq-IEq2 recovers the memory-free classical model, whereas i n line-eq-IEq3 αne-eq-IEq3 represents nonlocal temporal dependence of increasing strength. Its epidemiological relevance should be assessed through sensitivity analysis, parameter estimation, and comparison with observed data. Recently, fractional optimal control theory has received considerable attention in mathematical biology and engineering40. The combination of fractional dynamics and optimal control allows the construction of realistic control strategies that account for memory-dependent disease behavior while minimizing intervention costs. Several important developments in fractional optimal control systems were established in41–43. Applications involving epidemic systems, cancer dynamics, and quantum systems, dark mater in cosmological models demonstrated the efficiency of fractional optimal control formulations44–48. Despite the large number of studies devoted to hantavirus transmission dynamics, very few works considered fractional-order optimal control formulations for hantavirus systems. Most existing models are formulated using classical differential equations without incorporating memory effects or optimal intervention strategies. Moreover, the combined effects of rodent reduction, environmental sanitation, and treatment controls within a fractional-order framework remain insufficiently investigated. Recent studies have demonstrated the value of combining fractional-order operators with biologically structured transmission mechanisms, parameter estimation, threshold analysis, and optimal control. Caputo fractional models have been developed for foot-and-mouth disease with environmental transmission and intervention strategies, as well as for norovirus transmission with vaccination and an environmental reservoir49,50. These studies illustrate how memory effects and environmental persistence can be incorporated into infectious- disease systems. Fractional rabies models have also provided several relevant methodological developments. Caputo models calibrated through Markov chain Monte Carlo methods have been used to estimate uncertain transmission parameters and evaluate public-health interventions51. Related investigations have considered dog vaccination within a Caputo framework52, and rabies dynamics formulated with the Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo derivative and MCMC parameter estimation53. Comparative analyses of singular and nonsingular fractional operators have further clarified how alternative memory kernels influence epidemic trajectories54. Moreover, fractional optimal control and cost-effectiveness analysis have been applied to rabies interventions, demonstrating the practical importance of combining memory-dependent dynamics with intervention design55. Several recent works have also strengthened the theoretical foundation of fractional epidemic modeling. In a related study, a fractional epidemiological model incorporating vaccination and quarantine compartments was analyzed with respect to well-posedness, threshold behavior, stability, and optimal intervention56. Viral particles released from rodent excreta become aerosolized and may be inhaled by humans, leading to respiratory infection. The inset illustrates microscopic viral particles associated with the transmission pathway11. Fractional optimal control has also been applied to other nonlinear biological systems, including cancer–obesity dynamics, illustrating the broader applicability of Pontryagin-type methods in memory-dependent models58. Recent data-informed studies further highlight the importance of model calibration and uncertainty assessment. A fractional trachoma model calibrated with epidemiological data from Cameroon demonstrated how the fractional order can be estimated and interpreted using real observations59. Although the latter concerns plant disease, its mathematical framework remains relevant to the analysis of nonlinear disease systems. Taken together, these contributions support the use of fractional calculus, sensitivity analysis, and data-based estimation in infectious-disease modeling. The present work differs by focusing on hantavirus transmission between a persistent rodent reservoir and dead-end human hosts, while simultaneously incorporating rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans within a unified fractional optimal control framework. Motivated by these observations, this paper develops a new fractional optimal control model for hantavirus transmission dynamics between rodents and humans. The proposed model extends the classical hantavirus transmission framework by introducing Caputo fractional derivatives to capture hereditary effects in the disease dynamics. Three control variables are incorporated representing rodent elimination, environmental sanitation, and treatment efforts for infected individuals. Novelty of the study. The novelty of the present study lies in extending existing hantavirus transmission models in three connected directions. First, unlike classical integer-order models that describe rodent–human transmission without temporal memory, the proposed system uses the Caputo fractional derivative to represent hereditary and history-dependent effects. Second, the model integrates three intervention mechanisms— rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans—within a single optimal control framework. Third, the study provides a complete analytical and computational treatment, including positivity, boundedness, existence and uniqueness, equilibrium and stability analysis, the fractional Pontryagin optimality system, and a comparative assessment of no-control, single-control, and combined-control strategies. To the best of our knowledge, this combination has not been developed previously for hantavirus transmission between rodents and humans. Aim of the study. The main aim of this study is to develop and analyze a fractional optimal control model for hantavirus transmission between rodents and humans. The proposed model extends the classical SIR–SIR hantavirus framework by replacing the integer-order time derivative with the Caputo fractional derivative. This extension allows the model to account for memory effects, hereditary behavior, and the influence of past infection history on the current disease dynamics. The study also aims to design effective intervention strategies that reduce the number of infected humans and infected rodents while minimizing the cost of control implementation. To achieve this goal, three time- dependent controls are introduced: rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans. The mathematical analysis focuses on positivity, boundedness, existence, uniqueness, equilibrium behavior, and stability of the fractional model. In addition, Pontryagin’s maximum principle is used to derive the necessary optimality conditions, including the adjoint system and explicit control characterizations. A further aim is to investigate the numerical behavior of the model under different control scenarios and different fractional orders. The numerical simulations compare the uncontrolled case, single-control strategies, and combined optimal controls. This comparison helps identify the most effective strategy for reducing hantavirus transmission and highlights the role of the fractional-order parameter in producing smoother and more realistic epidemic trajectories. Innovation and applications The present study introduces a fractional optimal control framework for hantavirus transmission between rodents and humans. The innovation of the work lies in combining fractional-order epidemic modeling, rodent– human transmission dynamics, and optimal control theory in one unified mathematical structure. Unlike classical integer-order models, the proposed system uses the Caputo fractional derivative to describe memory-dependent disease evolution. This allows the model to account for past environmental exposure, previous rodent density, and accumulated contamination effects. Such effects are important in hantavirus transmission because the infection process depends not only on the current number of infected rodents but also on past ecological and epidemiological conditions. The main innovations of this work are summarized as follows: • A fractional SIR–SIR hantavirus transmission model is formulated for both human and rodent populations. • The Caputo fractional derivative is used to incorporate memory and hereditary effects into the epidemic dynamics. • Three realistic control strategies are introduced: rodent culling, sanitation, and treatment. • The model combines reservoir control, exposure reduction, and clinical intervention in a single optimal con­ trol problem. • Positivity, boundedness, existence, and uniqueness of solutions are established. • The basic reproduction number is analyzed to describe the persistence or elimination of infection. • Pontryagin’s maximum principle is applied to derive the adjoint system and the explicit characterization of optimal controls. • A fractional Adams–Bashforth–Moulton scheme with a forward–backward sweep method is used to solve the optimality system. Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:31685 4 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-72549-0 www.nature.com/scientificreports • Several numerical scenarios are compared to identify the most effective control policy. • The influence of the fractional-order parameter inline-eq-IEq4 is studied to show the role of memory effects in disease progression. The proposed model has several practical applications. It can help public health authorities evaluate different intervention strategies before implementation. It can also support decision-making in areas where hantavirus infection is linked to rodent density, environmental contamination, and limited healthcare resources. The rodent culling control inline-eq-IEq5 can guide policies related to trapping, poisoning, habitat destruction, and rodent population monitoring. The sanitation control inline-eq-IEq6 can support cleaning campaigns, safe waste removal, protection of food storage areas, and reduction of human exposure to rodent excreta. The treatment control inline-eq-IEq7 can help assess the impact of clinical care, hospitalization, and recovery-support programs. The numerical results show that combined optimal controls provide the strongest reduction in infected humans and infected rodents. This suggests that hantavirus control should not depend on a single intervention. A practical control program should combine reservoir reduction, environmental sanitation, and clinical treatment. From a mathematical viewpoint, the study contributes to fractional epidemic control theory by extending optimal control methods to a zoonotic disease model with two interacting populations. From an epidemiological viewpoint, it provides a flexible tool for studying hantavirus transmission under memory-dependent dynamics. analysis_zh.background: 本研究针对 汉坦病毒 在啮齿动物与人类之间的传播,这是一种致死率高且地理分布扩大的动物源性疾病。
analysis_zh.methods: 构建了包含 Caputo 分数导数的改进 SIR–SIR 模型,纳入啮齿动物扑杀、环境卫生和人类治疗作为时间依赖的控制措施;并证明了模型的正性和唯一性等数学性质。

analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究展示了分数阶微积分如何细化 汉坦病毒 的传播模型并优化控制措施,强调在针对特定疫情应用前需进行经验校准。
analysis_zh.limitations: 该模型缺乏基于真实监测数据的经验校准和验证,限制了其即时的预测效用。

papers.title: Epidemiology and Economic Burden of Puumala Virus Infection in Styria, Austria, 2003 to 2024.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and impose a potential burden on healthcare systems. However, comprehensive economic data remain scarce. We quantified the inpatient economic burden of hospitalized patients with Puumala virus (PUUV) infections in Styria, Austria's primary endemic region, to identify hospitalization costs and early admission predictors of costs. METHODS: This retrospective cost-of-illness study analyzed 1049 serologically confirmed PUUV hospitalizations across 20 public hospitals in Styria, Austria between September 2003 and March 2024. Costs were estimated using the Austrian performance-oriented hospital financing (Leistungsorientierte Krankenanstaltenfinanzierung) diagnosis-related group system, standardized to 2024-equivalent Euros using consumer price index deflation. Admission predictors of cost were assessed using multivariable γ-generalized linear modeling with multiple imputations. Temporal trends in length of stay were analyzed using weighted segmented linear regression. RESULTS: Cumulative inpatient cost was ∼€10.3 million (mean per-case: €9788) for the entire study period of 21 years. Three epidemic years (2012, 2019, and 2021) accounted for 53.6% of cases and over €5.2 million in expenditure, with peak annual costs reaching €1.93 million (0.274% of total Styrian inpatient expenditure) in 2012. Prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT; cost-ratio 1.024 per second, 95% CI 1.019-1.030) and older age (CR 1.004 per year, 95% CI 1.001-1.008) were independent admission-level predictors of higher cost. Median hospital length of stay declined by ∼50% over the study period. CONCLUSIONS: PUUV hospitalizations impose a sharply episodic but recurrent economic burden on regional healthcare systems. Admission aPTT and age independently predicted cost, but clinical outcomes were not modeled and these variables do not constitute a triage tool. Epidemic preparedness strategies are warranted.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and impose a potential burden on healthcare systems (A1).
analysis.methods: Retrospective cost‑of‑illness study of 1,049 serologically confirmed PUUV hospitalizations across 20 public hospitals in Styria, Austria (Sept 2003–Mar 2024) (A4); costs estimated via Austrian DRG system standardized to 2024 € (A5); admission cost predictors assessed with multivariable γ‑GLM and multiple imputation (A6); length‑of‑stay trends analyzed by weighted segmented linear regression (A7).
analysis.results: Cumulative inpatient cost was ~€10.3 M (mean €9 788 per case) over 21 years (A8); three epidemic years (2012, 2019, 2021) accounted for 53.6% of cases and >€5.2 M, with a peak annual cost of €1.93 M in 2012 (0.274% of Styrian inpatient expenditure) (A9); prolonged aPTT (cost‑ratio 1.024 s⁻¹, 95 % CI 1.019‑1.030) and older age (CR 1.004 yr⁻¹, 95 % CI 1.001‑1.008) were independent cost predictors (A11); median hospital length of stay declined ~50% over the period (A12).
analysis.contribution: Quantifies the episodic economic impact of PUUV hospitalizations in a regional endemic area and identifies admission‑level cost predictors, informing budgeting and epidemic preparedness (A13‑A15).
analysis.limitations: Comprehensive economic data remain scarce (A2); clinical outcomes were not modeled and cost predictors do not constitute a triage tool; conclusions are based on abstract‑only information (evidence_scope).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and may burden healthcare systems. Methods: A retrospective cost‑of‑illness analysis of 1,049 serologically confirmed Puumala virus hospitalizations across 20 public hospitals in Styria, Austria (Sept 2003–Mar 2024) used Austrian DRG costing standardized to 2024 €, multivariable γ‑GLM with multiple imputation for cost predictors, and weighted segmented linear regression for length‑of‑stay trends. Results: Total inpatient cost was ≈€10.3 M (mean €9 788 per case); three epidemic years (2012, 2019, 2021) contributed 53.6% of cases and >€5.2 M, with a peak annual cost of €1.93 M in 2012 (0.274% of Styrian inpatient spending); prolonged aPTT (cost‑ratio 1.024 s⁻¹, 95 % CI 1.019‑1.030) and older age (CR 1.004 yr⁻¹, 95 % CI 1.001‑1.008) independently predicted higher costs; median length of stay fell ~50% over the period. Contribution: Provides the first regional quantification of PUUV hospitalization economic burden and identifies admission‑level cost predictors, supporting budgeting and preparedness planning. Limitations: Comprehensive economic data are scarce, clinical outcomes were not modeled, and findings are based on abstract‑only information.

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒感染导致肾综合征出血热,并对医疗系统构成潜在负担 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 回顾性疾病成本研究,涉及奥地利斯蒂里亚地区20家公立医院在2003年9月至2024年3月期间的1,049例血清学确诊PUUV住院病例 (A4);费用通过奥地利DRG系统估算并标准化至2024年欧元 (A5);入院费用预测因子采用多变量γ-GLM和多重插补评估 (A6);住院时长趋势使用加权分段线性回归分析 (A7)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 量化了区域流行区PUUV住院的阶段性经济影响,并识别了入院层面的费用预测因子,为预算编制和疫情防备提供依据 (A13‐A15)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 全面的经济数据仍然稀缺 (A2);临床结局未建模,费用预测因子并非分诊工具;结论基于仅有的摘要信息 (evidence_scope)。
